abstract_text: Whether generative AI (GenAI) use helps or hinders critical thinking remains contested, and existing accounts emphasize exposure to the tool rather than how a person structures their engagement with it. Extending Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory to human-AI partnerships, we test a structural account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted academic work among 891 college students in the United States and Türkiye. Self-appraised thinking ability and confidence in the partnership shaped how much practical experience a person built up with GenAI, but neither predicted critical thinking directly. abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. summary.finding: Requests accounted for 81.5% of coded turns. title: Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning
preview: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly explored as collaborative learning partners in mathematics education, yet it remains unclear what makes an AI recognizable as a peer. This study examines how domain experts perceive and interact with an adaptive LLM-based peer agent combining a Big Five-informed persona with motivational state modulation for collaborative mathematics problem solving. abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly explored as collaborative learning partners in mathematics education, yet it remains unclear what makes an AI recognizable as a peer. This study examines how domain experts perceive and interact with an adaptive LLM-based peer agent combining a Big Five-informed persona with motivational state modulation for collaborative mathematics problem solving. Through thematic analysis of expert interviews, we identify conditions shaping peer perceptions, including emotional safety, shared control, and collaborative reasoning. Participants primarily judged the AI through its social behavior rather than mathematical capabilities. analysis.methods: Before the formal study, we conducted a pilot study with two experts in educational technology. The pilot aimed to validate the clarity of the study scenario, the realism of the agent’s behavior, and the usability of the design. Participants in the pilot interacted with the agent and provided open-ended feedback on the interaction flow, personality expression, and perceived peer-likeness. Data from the pilot study were not included in the analysis. We adopted an exploratory qualitative approach to examine how the theory-informed AI peer design was experienced and interpreted in interaction [8]. The initial design was grounded in theories of peer learning and social interaction, and the study aimed to understand how these theoretical principles translated into the agent’s interactional behaviors and how they were perceived during use. Rather than testing learning outcomes, we focused on identifying interactional patterns, tensions, and characteristics that could inform the development of a framework for designing AI agents as We conducted the qualitative study between December 2025 and January 2026 with seven researchers in User Experience, Learning Sciences, Educational Technology, and Computer Science, with experience ranging from 3 to over 20 years. Participants were asked to critically engage with the AI agent as a peer and examine how the proposed design dimensions manifested during interaction. In particular, we explored how participants interpreted the agent’s social role, perceived its position of authority, and identified moments of collaboration, role shifts, or interactional breakdown. The study was approved by the university ethics board, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Each session lasted approximately 30 minutes and was conducted through an online meeting platform. After consent, participants were asked to take the perspective of a student learning quadratic functions. Participants then interacted with the AI agent for approximately 20 minutes to collaboratively solve quadratic equations (Figure 2). They received the same information about quadratic functions that had been provided during the agent’s development and were encouraged to treat the agent as a classmate and reason collaboratively, rather than expecting direct instruction or final answers. No specific conversational structure was imposed so as to preserve the natural development of the interaction. Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning 7 Following the interaction, participants completed a structured interview based on predefined questions derived from the research questions. The interview focused on how they interpreted the agent’s social role and authority, how the interaction reflected the proposed design dimensions, and where they observed moments of collaboration, role shifts, All sessions were audio-recorded with participants’ permission and transcribed. The interview transcripts were de- identified before analysis. We conducted an iterative thematic analysis [31]. Two authors independently reviewed the transcripts, generated initial codes, and then collaboratively grouped them into themes, through discussion and Fig. 2. analysis.results: 5.1 RQ1: Perception of an AI peer agent 5.1.1 Reduced Pressure and Increased Safety. A dominant theme across the interviews was that participants associated a stronger sense of safety with interacting with the AI compared to a real peer, when considering the experience from a learner’s perspective. This allowed them to focus on the math problem without worrying about being judged. P1 explained that when compared to regular class setting, seeing other students finish faster made them feel “anxious and ashamed," while with the AI there was no comparison. P3 shared that because the agent was “not a real human being," they felt “less embarrassed" and “more comfortable making mistakes"; P5 also emphasized that safety came from the lack of human judgment: “I know he won’t think I’m fool...He doesn’t have any human emotions, he’s just AI." P6 further explained that safety increased when the AI felt like an equal. They suggested that if the agent was presented as ”your classmate...same level as you," then “it feels safer", as “with your friend or someone equal to you, you can make mistakes without a problem." This shows that safety was created both by the AI’s non-human nature and by the feeling 8 Yiran Lin, Ye Deng, Ziqi Pan, Yongan Yu, and Alexandra I. Cristea of equality. For these participants, experiencing the AI as a peer meant being able to make mistakes without fear of 5.1.2 Peer Through Imperfection.Participants described the AI’s peer-likeness through its willingness to acknowledge its own imperfections, which are caused by the inherent imperfections of LLM. P3 felt the agent was peer-like because it was “not very clever" and made “stupid and simple mistakes." When P3 gave a wrong answer and the agent accepted it, they said it felt “like a real human peer." P7 expressed a similar view; the agent felt like a peer, as it “did not show the solution directly," but instead “made some assumptions and asked for my idea." They also noted that the agent “made mistakes sometimes" and tried wrong approaches before asking for participants’ opinion, which made the interaction However, not all participants welcomed this behavior. P5 disliked an AI that was “as stupid as I am," and believed a peer should be “smarter than me" to provide helpful ideas. This shows that while mistakes helped some participants see the AI as human-like, others felt that too many mistakes reduced its usefulness. This indicates a distinction between peer-likeness and peer-usefulness, which were not always aligned in participants’ experiences. 5.1.3 The Impact of Personality and Motivation Embeddings.Personality and motivation had different effects on participants. P1 felt the agent’s personality was “steady" and that it “really wants me to learn," which made the interaction feel meaningful. However, P7 did not experience the personality as stable. They said it was “more a surface level" and changed according to the user’s input. They added that they mainly saw the AI “as a tool, not ... with personality... like friends." This shows that for some participants, the personality design was not strong enough. Personality also caused problems when the tone felt inappropriate. P1 became anxious when the agent said it was “feeling a bit unconcerned," which sounded dismissive. Others described the agent as “strict" (P4) or a “know-it-all" (P2). When the agent sounded confident or directive, participants were more likely to see it as a teacher rather than a peer. This shows that personality can help create consistency, but it can also create distance, if the tone is too authoritative. 5.1.4 Collaboration versus Instruction.Participants described collaboration as situations where the AI guided their thinking without taking control. P6 felt like “working together as a team" because the agent “has the information but . . . gives you hints and lets you think and be part of the solution." This feeling changed when the AI moved too quickly. P7 felt “a little annoyed" when they were still thinking and the agent “just gave me the right number." For them, showing the answer too early broke the sense of collaboration. Similarly, P4 felt the agent was “examining me, not helping me," and P2 said it was “very fixed on a direction of travel." In these moments, the AI was no longer seen as a peer, but as a tutor giving instructions. In summary, participants experienced the AI as a peer when it supported their thinking process, and as a teacher when it controlled the pace or 5.2 RQ2: Boundaries of AI as a learning peer 5.2.1 Failure of Shared Memory and Mutual Understanding.The most significant boundary emerged through moments of confusion, where the AI failed to maintain a consistent shared understanding. For a peer relationship to be effective, both partners must remember what was previously discussed. P2 expressed frustration when the agent “claims I’ve said some things which I didn’t," which led to a direct “breakdown in trust". P3 experienced a similar issue at the very start of the conversation, when the agent assumed they were already solving an equation that hadn’t been introduced yet. P3 remarked, “I don’t remember anything about giving an equation... its previous memory might prevent our mutual Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning 9 understanding." These point to a boundary that the AI cannot yet act as a reliable, long-term peer, because it often hallucinates or mixes up different conversations. 5.2.2 Blind Validation and Misinformation.Another boundary appeared through discomfort when the AI agreed with incorrect ideas. P4 asked, "Is he agreeing because it’s correct or because he doesn’t know the correct answer?" P2 warned that this could “keep reinforcing those mistakes forever.” P7 believed this issue came from the design rather than from the idea of an AI peer, “I would rather say it’s due to the design... if it can hold on and not show the correct answer.” This shows that participants accepted the idea of an AI peer, but expected better control over how and when 5.2.3 Lack of Flexibility. Resistance emerged when the AI enforced a fixed problem-solving order. P5 said the agent “doesn’t want me to jump the steps." P2 felt it did not “really try and collaborate" with their ideas. P7 also suggested that the agent should wait longer before giving answers. Overall, AI was seen as less peer-like when it followed a rigid process, instead of adapting to the participants’ approach. 5.2.4 Emotional and Social Gaps.Finally, participants noted that the AI could not respond well to their emotions. P1 said the agent could not “sense your tone, your emotions or motivations," and sometimes sounded “harsh or abrupt.” When the agent said it was unconcerned,” P1 felt more stressed. analysis.discussion: This study responds to the growing attention in AIED that looks beyond designing AI systems merely as instructional tools. We examined how learners experience an AI agent in the social–cognitive role of a peer, laying the groundwork for future research on AI systems that emulate human-like social and cognitive behaviors in learning environments. Our findings show that in peer-oriented designs, correctness alone is insufficient; the enactment of authority, uncertainty, and shared responsibility is central. We contribute a human-centered set of design and evaluation dimensions for AI peer agents that emphasize interaction quality, emotional safety, and shared control. This perspective clarifies AI peers not as simplified tutors or information providers, but as partners that support collaborative reasoning and sustained engagement.

abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. reading.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
reading.findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
reading.interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
reading.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Cognitive Scaffolding, Substitution, and the Risk of Deskilling
preview:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining appro…
abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

Among the retained features, stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) exhibited the strongest positive predictive effects on academic impact, indicating that these two factors are the most prominent behavioral signals of impaired academic functioning in adolescents. Number of notifications (coefficient = 0.213) and number of application openings (coefficient = 0.186) also entered the model, suggesting that frequent digital interruptions, rather than total screen time per se, may represent a key mechanism underlying the erosion of academic attention. This finding is consistent with the central premise of interruption theory, which posits that frequent task switching and attentional interruptions significantly impair cognitive task efficiency and performance (Oulasvirta and Salovaara, 2004; Oulasvirta and Saariluoma, 2006) . Notably, work and study time (coefficient = -0.152) and sleep duration (coefficient = -0.109) exhibited negative coefficients, indicating that adequate study time and sufficient sleep were negatively associated with academic impairment even within a digitally intensive environment. Age (coefficient = -0.087) and weekend screen time (coefficient = 0.074) had relatively small coefficients, suggesting limited predictive utility of demographic variables and time-specific behavioral differences. The variable selection results of LASSO not only reduced model complexity but also provided a focused feature set for subsequent network analysis and machine learning modeling.

The number of notifications exhibited prominent bridge centrality, indicating that external environmental distractions play an important cross-community connecting role. Third, the XGBoost model achieved a predictive performance with an AUC of 0.842, confirming the effective predictive capacity of attention-related features for academic impact. The SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern, with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 h for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear pattern for stress level, consistent with a threshold-like pattern of association between social media use duration and academic impact. Fourth, latent profile analysis identified three heterogeneous subgroups, among which the "high stress-exhaustion" group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%, indicating that the combination of high stress and insufficient sleep constitutes the pattern most strongly associated with the most severe academic impairment. The above findings have clear practical implications for the prevention and intervention of academic impact in adolescents. First, school-based mental health education should incorporate stress management as a core component of the curriculum and establish routine stress screening mechanisms to identify adolescents under high stress and provide timely psychological support. Second, interventions targeting digital media use should not adopt a one-sizefits-all approach of simply limiting screen time. Instead, attention should be paid to the modifiability of external distraction factors such as push notifications, and for those who have already reached high levels of social media use, cognitive-behavioral training focusing on self-regulation skills and time management should be emphasized. Third, based on the three subgroups identified by latent profile analysis, a stratified intervention approach is recommended: the "low-risk type" should receive preventive education, the "high digital exposure type" should focus on habit restructuring and self-monitoring training, and the "high stress-exhaustion type" requires multidisciplinary comprehensive interventions integrating mental health care, sleep hygiene, and digital use management. title: ChatGPT as cognitive scaffold: computational thinking and metacognition in AI-embedded instruction
preview: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one …
abstract_text: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

abstract_text: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this impairment, particularly in response to sleep-related stimuli, remain unclear. A total of 48 participants, comprising 24 individuals with insomnia disorder (ID) and 24 healthy controls (HC), were recruited to perform a modified task-switching paradigm incorporating sleep-related (e.g., bed) and general stimuli during functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) scanning. Behavioral measures (reaction time, accuracy, and switch cost), task activation and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI)-based task-dependent functional connectivity were analyzed. Two subjective questionaires, the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory and the Insomnia Severity Index were collectely simultaneously. The ID group exhibited significantly lower CFI scores compared to the HC group, indicating subjective cognitive flexibility impairment. Notably, in the task-switching performance, the ID group demonstrated faster reaction times to sleep-related stimuli. fMRI results revealed altered activation in the right precuneus, angular gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus, with interaction effects between group and stimulus type. The gPPI analyses showed that, compared to HC, ID group exhibited enhanced connectivity between the precuneus and cerebellar under sleep stimulus conditions, as well as disrupted connectivity between the angular gyrus and frontal-parietal regions, and reduced integration from the superior temporal gyrus to multiple association regions across networks. These findings suggest that insomnia is characterized by both subjective deficits in cognitive flexibility and altered neural network dynamics during task switching, with sleep-related stimuli exerting a significant modulatory effect. Enhanced attention captured by sleep-related information may interfere with the optimal task-related network coordination, providing a potential mechanism linking insomnia to executive dysfunction. abstract_text: Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) typically perform cognitive tasks with greater response time variability than matched peers. This is thought to be due to the greater occurrence of occasional extremely slow responses associated with lowered arousal levels. To test this we designed a new, less arousing task to measure sustained attention, named the Disappearance Detection Task (DDT). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between response time variability and levels of ADHD symptoms both in this new, low-arousal sustained attention task and in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). Twenty-eight children and 49 adolescents participated. On both tasks, ADHD symptom levels were associated with response time variability measures of SDRT and tau, but not with sigma. On the DDT, children with higher ADHD symptoms made more commission errors and were less accurate in detecting the target (d'), whereas adolescents made a similar number of commission errors and d' irrespective of their ADHD symptom levels. This pattern was not present in the SART. The adolescents found the DDT more challenging than the SART as their target sensitivity was lower during the DDT. The children were less confident in nominating the target (criterion) during the DDT than the SART. The results indicate that RTV measures are more consistently associated with ADHD symptoms than other RT measures and that the DDT is a sensitive task of sustained attention and response inhibition performance, particularly in children, and in children with higher symptoms of ADHD.

title: Between Human and Machine: University Teachers’ Accounts of Judgment, Metacognitive Defense, and Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI Use
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

Participants were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling within a learning community devoted to AI-empowered teaching, to which the first author belongs. The community was founded in December 2023, with the purpose of discussing and sharing emerging GenAI tools and creative uses among university teachers and doctoral students. Teachers who had considered GenAI and rejected it, and teachers who had never encountered it, are not represented. This was an insider study: the first author and most participants belong to the same learning community that was open to rolling recruitment, and some interviews and self-narratives were produced during community events. This position afforded trust, contextual understanding and access to naturalistic accounts. Within this sample, teachers shifted the defense of professional value from “what I know” towards “what I can judge”: verification and judgment carry clear evidence in 24 of the 25 cases, and irreplaceability construction appears in 24 of 25. The closest analogue lies outside education: newsrooms incorporating generative AI have likewise relocated professional authority from the production of content to its authentication ( Ashuri et al., 2026 ). What distinguishes the present case is that judgment is claimed not only as a competence but as a position in a professional self-description, expressed through labels such as “gatekeeper”, “goalie”, “navigator” and “auditor”. In Biesta et al. ’s ( 2015 ) terms, these labels name a capacity participants claim they can still exercise under the conditions they face, which is what makes them serviceable for identity work. The strategies described in Section 4.3.1 —independence first, retaining the right to err, forced thinking, and attention management—can be interpreted as boundary work: participants repeatedly drew a line around “whose cognition” was engaged in a task, seeking to prevent cognitive offloading from becoming cognitive dependence. Comparable boundary work has been documented where professionals must decide how far to let an algorithmic recommendation stand in for their own judgment ( Li, 2026 ). This interpretation is consistent with the cognitive-offloading literature: offloading is not inherently harmful, but its consequences depend on how it is monitored ( Risko & Gilbert, 2016 ). Experimental work raises concerns about reduced regulatory effort in some GenAI-supported tasks ( Fan et al., 2025 ), while observational and review evidence links offloading with variation in critical thinking and learner agency ( Gerlich, 2025 ; G. Wang et al., 2026 ). These sources do not establish a uniform causal effect of AI use. That these consequences vary across users ( Si et al., 2026 ) lends empirical weight to the conditionalist position articulated by 11 of the 25 teacher cases. The participants’ accounts resembled norms of “monitored offloading” (human-in-the-loop; quality dependence). Their use of agency (zhutixing) to justify these practices also connected cognitive strategy with educational ethics—both a practical stance and a belief summarized as “Above AI there is still the human”. Teachers’ AI-related beliefs—instrumental or partnership, boundary beliefs, identity beliefs—appear to orient cognitive strategies such as verification, calibration, defense and reflection. These strategies encounter feedback in practice, including efficiency gains, hallucination-related failures, student plagiarism, and additional workload. Participants’ retrospective accounts locate belief revision at nodes they describe as turning points, after which revised beliefs support new strategies. The security narratives of Section 4.1.3 are interpreted as an affective dimension of this arrangement. We present the figure as an interpretation of retrospective, cross-sectional, self-reported accounts and as a hypothesis for longitudinal research. The arrows record what participants describe as following from what, not tested directions of effect, and nothing in the design permits a claim that one element produces another; establishing that would require following teachers over time and observing what they do rather than what they report. Taken together, the three themes suggest that these accounts may represent a form of collective identity work rather than isolated individual adjustment. Participants shared a vocabulary (gatekeeping, agency, irreplaceability), a metaphor repertoire (passenger seat, mirror, goalie, filter), and a narrative arc. Membership of a common learning community is a competing explanation for that convergence, not merely a limitation on its generalization: people who talk to one another regularly about a shared problem come to describe it in shared terms, and part of what we report may be the circulation of a vocabulary rather than the independent arrival of 25 teachers at the same position. Three features of the sample bear on how the findings should be taken. Every participant was already engaged with GenAI, which is why disenchantment appears here as a stage within continued use rather than as grounds for abandonment. Foreign-language teachers make up 10 of the 25 cases, which is likely to be one reason the erosion of a disciplinary skill base is so prominent. And the protocol introduced several of the propositions at issue. At the same time, the prominence of “learning from accomplished people” (Teacher V), “teaching is the best learning”, and “mutual inspiration” (Teacher Y) indicates that peer exchange may function as infrastructure for teacher development in the AI era. Comparative work with teachers outside such communities is needed to establish whether these patterns extend further. Research on cognitive offloading examines how external resources change demands on memory, monitoring and task performance ( Risko & Gilbert, 2016 ). analysis.limitations: Drawing on multi-source qualitative materials from 25 university teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks, this study examined how they describe their beliefs about GenAI and the cognitive strategies they use alongside it. Four conclusions follow. First, participants described a broadly shared boundary around what AI cannot do—emotion, embodiment, metacognition, tacit knowledge, judgment—which served both to make sense of the technology and to protect a professional position; this boundary was elicited by a direct question and should be taken as the shape of their answers to it. Second, participants commonly reconstructed the teacher role from “knowledge transmitter” towards “guide, designer, companion, gatekeeper”, in terms they volunteered, while ten of the 25 cases (40.0%) retained a reinterpreted claim to expertise. Third, judgment and gatekeeping were re-centered as the defended core of professional work, with verification and judgment carrying clear evidence in 24 of 25 cases. Fourth, participants described managing cognitive participation on both sides of the desk, taking divergent positions on “intellectual degeneration” (9 endorsement, 11 conditional, 2 rebuttal, 1 ambivalent, 2 no position) while describing a varied repertoire of defensive strategies with differing levels of explicit support. The relation between belief and cognition that these accounts suggest is reciprocal but not demonstrated: it is an interpretation of what teachers say, offered for longitudinal and observational examination. The contribution to research on intelligence lies in connecting teachers’ own cognitive offloading with the learning conditions they report designing for others. Professional judgment and metacognitive regulation are central to these accounts, but their effectiveness requires observational and learning-outcome evidence. The study carries implications for teachers and institutions. On the one hand, professional development in the AI era could move beyond “learning to use tools” toward “cultivating judgment”, including the disciplinary expertise needed to verify AI output, the metacognitive habit of monitoring cognitive participation, and the willingness “to err personally.” Teacher L’s phrase captures this emphasis: “AI gives the skeleton; the human fills in the soul.” On the other hand, teacher participants reported that AI had not reduced but increased their burden, and described assessment as a domain in which established practices had lost their force without replacements being available. Institutions could respond by supporting instructional-design experimentation, clarifying academic-integrity standards, and creating a fault-tolerant environment in which teachers can test and evaluate new practices, rather than limiting support to tool training. Regardless, the study is not without limitations. First, the sample was a purposive and snowball sample of teachers already engaged with GenAI, recruited through a common learning community and its professional networks, and the findings cannot be generalized to Chinese university teachers as a whole; the beliefs of resistant and avoidant teachers are not represented, and the community’s shared vocabulary cannot be separated from the convergence we report. Second, the analysis relied on self-reports, so the relation between stated beliefs and classroom practice requires observational evidence. Third, the design is largely cross-sectional and retrospective and cannot establish trajectories or directions of effect. Fourth, broad code definitions and shared interview prompts can increase coverage without establishing independently shared beliefs. The agreement check covers a small sample of meaning units and does not validate all case-level evidence ratings. English translations did not receive an additional bilingual check. Finally, the cases rest on uneven combinations of interviews, self-narratives, published essays, field notes, chat records, product documents and recorded AI dialogues; three cases (D, E, F) rest on documentary material without an interview, and an absent code in a thinly documented case records the limits of the material rather than the absence of a belief.

title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

analysis.discussion: This systematic review examined the psychological processes through which learners engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in foreign language education. Drawing on 51 empirical studies, it moved beyond whether GenAI improves particular language skills to examine how learners understand, evaluate, regulate, and coordinate their interactions with generative systems. Metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation emerged as interconnected mechanisms underlying GenAI-mediated learning, while AI literacy and learner agency functioned as enabling conditions. The findings conceptualize learning with GenAI as adaptive human-AI partnership. Metacognition supports goal setting, monitoring of AI contributions, evaluation, and subsequent regulation. Trust calibration shapes decisions about whether AI-generated information or feedback should be accepted, verified, modified, or rejected. Human-AI co-regulation captures the distribution and coordination of cognitive and regulatory work between learners and AI. These mechanisms are neither discrete nor strictly sequential; rather, they form a dynamic system in which metacognitive evaluation informs trust and reliance, reliance shapes cognitive distribution, and interaction outcomes provide new information for subsequent regulation. The educational value of GenAI therefore depends less on its capacity to generate language, provide feedback, or perform cognitive tasks than on how learners incorporate these affordances into their regulatory activity. GenAI can augment learning when learners retain responsibility for planning, evaluation, judgment, and reflection. When these functions are increasingly delegated to AI, assistance may become cognitive substitution, potentially weakening independent engagement and learner control. Productive augmentation and problematic dependence thus depend primarily on how cognitive and regulatory responsibility is organized. The Metacognition-Trust-Co-Regulation (MTC) Framework integrates these processes into a unified theoretical account. It explains how cognitive activity can be distributed between learners and AI while preserving human agency as the organizing principle of learning. AI literacy and learner agency are conceptualized not as additional MTC mechanisms but as enabling conditions that help learners understand GenAI's capabilities and limitations, calibrate reliance, and retain ownership of learning. The framework therefore provides a basis for explaining variation in psychological and learning outcomes, including autonomy, motivation, confidence, engagement, cognitive load, feedback literacy, and agency. The principal contribution of this review is to specify the psychological conditions under which GenAI becomes educationally productive, rather than characterizing it as inherently beneficial or detrimental. This perspective shifts attention from evaluating GenAI primarily as an instructional technology toward understanding how learners regulate its use while preserving the cognitive activities through which learning occurs. Future research should empirically test the MTC Framework across learner populations, language tasks, educational settings, and GenAI systems. Longitudinal, experimental, and processsensitive designs are needed to examine whether the proposed relationships among metacognition, trust, and co-regulation remain robust across contexts and over time. Research should also identify when human-AI cognitive partnerships enhance learning without displacing essential cognitive and regulatory activities. The central challenge for GenAI-enhanced foreign language education is not how much learning can be delegated to AI, but how AI can be integrated while preserving and strengthening learners' capacity to think, evaluate, regulate, and act independently.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. The 51 studies varied substantially in participants, research designs, learning contexts, AI applications, and operationalization's of psychological constructs, which limits direct comparison across studies. Moreover, the evidence base is relatively recent and rapidly evolving; findings associated with particular GenAI systems may therefore change as technologies and patterns of use develop. The review has methodological limitations related to its singleauthor design. Screening, full-text assessment, and thematic coding were conducted by the sole author without independent reviewer or coder verification, which may have introduced selection or interpretive bias despite the use of a structured coding framework and documented screening decisions. No formal risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted, reflecting the theory-building focus and methodological heterogeneity of the included studies. The database coverage also represents a limitation. Although Web of Science and Scopus provided broad multidisciplinary coverage, PsycINFO and ERIC were not searched. Future reviews should incorporate education and psychology-specific databases to broaden coverage and reduce potential database-related selection bias. Overall, the MTC Framework should be viewed as a theory-generating account that requires further empirical validation. The evidence also relied substantially on self-reports, interviews, surveys, and relatively short-term interventions. Although these approaches provide valuable insights into learners' perceptions and experiences, they may not fully capture how metacognitive regulation, trust calibration, and cognitive redistribution unfold during actual learner-AI interaction. Future research should therefore incorporate more longitudinal and process-sensitive approaches, including interaction logs, prompt histories, revision records, think-aloud protocols, and screen-based observation. Further research should examine how learner proficiency, prior AI experience, AI literacy, metacognitive ability, task complexity, instructional design, and teacher mediation shape MTC processes. In particular, the proposed framework requires empirical testing. Longitudinal, experimental, and mixed-methods research could examine whether metacognitive engagement is associated with trust calibration, whether calibrated reliance is associated with particular forms of co-regulation, and whether these processes are subsequently related to language-learning and psychological outcomes.

title: Designing generative AI–powered reflective learning dashboards for enhancing self-regulated learning in higher education
preview: A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. abstract_text:
A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. Using a quasi-experimental design, 180 undergraduate students participated in a 12-week intervention comparing traditional instructor feedback with AI-generated reflective feedback. Quantitative results revealed significant improvements in self-regulated learning behaviours, time on task, login frequency and academic performance (p < .001), indicating strong effects on both cognitive and behavioural dimensions of learning. In addition, students reported high levels of perceived usefulness, trust, personalisation and positive attitudes towards AI-generated feedback, supported by qualitative insights highlighting increased motivation and learner agency. The findings demonstrate that combining generative AI with learning analytics transforms feedback into a dynamic, dialogic process that enhances reflective thinking and adaptive learning. This study contributes a scalable, human-centred and ethically grounded model for improving both learning outcomes and learner experience in digital education environments.
 
Implications for practice or policy:

University administrators should implement transparent AI dashboards ensuring ethics, privacy and accountability.
Educators can enhance reflective learning by integrating adaptive AI feedback that supports metacognitive development.
Policymakers should promote AI literacy and self-regulated learning within higher education frameworks.
Technology developers need to design user-centred and interpretable AI systems aligned with pedagogical objectives.
Higher education leaders should foster AI-supported reflection, professional development and evidence-based innovation for sustainable transformation.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   Objective: Deficits in attention have been linked to poorer performance on executive functioning tasks, particularly those requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility. While continuous performance tests are commonly used to assess sustained attention, their relationship to error based executive outcomes under increased task demand in pediatric clinical populations remains incompletely characterized. This study examined whether performance on a relatively low demand task of sustained attention, the Conners’ Continuous Performance Test–Third Edition (CPT-3), predicts performance on a higher demand executive task, the Delis–Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS) Color Word Interference Test (CW). Method/Data Selection: Data were obtained from a mixed clinical sample of 213 children and adolescents ages 8–17 years (M = 11.7, SD = 2.8; 47.8% male, 52.2% female) evaluated in an outpatient private practice neuropsychology clinic. Participants completed the CPT-3 and D-KEFS CW as part of individualized comprehensive neuropsychological batteries. Multivariate regression analyses examined whether CPT-3 subscales predicted performance on D-KEFS CW conditions. Results/Data Synthesis: The overall model significantly predicted D-KEFS Inhibition Error scores (R2 = .12, adjusted R2 = .08, F(9, 198) = 3.02, p = .002) and D-KEFS Inhibition/Switching Error scores (R2 = .17, adjusted R2 = .13, F(9, 198) = 4.56, p &lt; .001). CPT-3 reaction time–based indices accounted for the majority of explained variance across both error outcomes. Conclusions: Performance on a sustained attention task was associated with error based executive performance requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility in this pediatric clinical sample. Faster response speed and higher variability in response speed may be linked more impulsive verbal responding, resulting in higher errors on a cognitively demanding task.

title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) confronts educational psychology with sharply heterogeneous evidence: meta-analyses report positive average effects on learning alongside prediction intervals spanning harm to benefit, and experiments document gains in some configurations and learning penalties in others. This article develops an augmentation–erosion framework that accounts for part of this heterogeneity by …
abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) confronts educational psychology with sharply heterogeneous evidence: meta-analyses report positive average effects on learning alongside prediction intervals spanning harm to benefit, and experiments document gains in some configurations and learning penalties in others. This article develops an augmentation–erosion framework that accounts for part of this heterogeneity by treating the educational effect of GenAI not as a property of the tool but as a property of the partition of cognitive labor between learner and machine. Integrating research on cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, and self-regulated learning, the framework holds that offloading augments learning when it discharges operations peripheral to the current learning goal, and risks erosion, whether of acquisition or of maintenance, when it bypasses the processing constitutive of that goal, unless the learner substantively processes the output or later reconstructs it. It supplies criteria for locating operations along a graded peripheral–constitutive continuum, specifies the comparison condition against which augmentation and erosion are defined, and states seven conditioned, testable propositions, each illustrated with a common example and paired with supporting and challenging patterns. On this basis, offloading regulation is proposed as a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy with domain-general and discipline-specific components: a competence comprising partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification, and re-internalization, enacted through metacognitive control and conditioned by learners’ goals and motivation. The article closes with an intervention research program, a measurement strategy that triangulates interaction logs with process measures, and equity implications, using STEM learning as a strategically revealing case.

title: Trust in Generative AI and Critical Thinking Among College Students: A Structural Equation Modeling Analysis Based on Perceived Usefulness, Cognitive Offloading, and AI Self-Efficacy
preview: This study examines how college students’ trust in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is associated with critical thinking engagement in GenAI-supported learning through multiple psychological mechanisms. Drawing on Distributed Cognition Theory (DCT), we propose and test a structural model including five constructs: trust in AI, perceived usefulness, cognitive offloading, AI self-efficacy, and critical think…
abstract_text: This study examines how college students’ trust in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is associated with critical thinking engagement in GenAI-supported learning through multiple psychological mechanisms. Drawing on Distributed Cognition Theory (DCT), we propose and test a structural model including five constructs: trust in AI, perceived usefulness, cognitive offloading, AI self-efficacy, and critical thinking. Drawing on survey data from a convenience sample of college students who engaged in learning activities using GenAI tools (e.g., ChatGPT), we assessed hypothesized relationships using structural equation modeling (SEM). The results show that trust in AI is positively associated with perceived usefulness and AI self-efficacy, and both constructs are positively associated with critical thinking. In contrast, cognitive offloading is negatively associated with critical thinking, indicating a potential constraining pathway through which stronger reliance on GenAI may be associated with lower engagement in higher-order thinking. Overall, the findings suggest that trust in GenAI is linked to critical thinking through both supportive and constraining pathways. This study extends DCT in GenAI-supported learning by showing that trust in AI is not uniformly beneficial. The findings highlight the importance of educational approaches that cultivate students’ efficacy beliefs and strategic use of GenAI while discouraging overreliance that reduces cognitive engagement.

abstract_text: This study examines how undergraduate students integrate generative AI tools into home exams and how these practices relate to self-regulated learning (SRL) and academic performance. Using a mixed-methods design, we analyzed exam responses, self-reports, and performance data from 891 students enrolled in BA-level qualitative methodology courses (2023–2024). Students were permitted to use AI if they disclosed their usage. Three modes of AI engagement were identified: instrumental (task completion with minimal evaluation), ideational (idea generation and selective integration), and reflective (critical evaluation and feedback-driven refinement). At a general level, AI use was associated with increased efficiency and somewhat higher performance than non-use. However, these aggregate patterns masked substantial variation across modes of use. Instrumental use was associated with weaker performance in some tasks, including definition tasks where reliance on generic AI-generated responses did not align with course-specific criteria. In contrast, reflective engagement with AI was associated with stronger and more consistent performance. Interpreted through an SRL framework, these findings suggest that outcomes of AI use depend on how students regulate its use. Rather than uniformly supporting or undermining learning, AI appears to amplify differences in students’ self-regulatory capacities. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing skills for critical and reflective engagement with AI.

analysis.methods: The study was conducted in the "Introduction to Qualitative Methods" course offered to undergraduate students in the Faculty of Social Sciences at the University of Eastern Finland. The compulsory course is taken in the second or third year by students in social sciences, health and social management, business, geography, and open university. Instruction and assessment were conducted in Finnish (quotes are translated into English). The dataset is based on a home exam consisting of three tasks. The first task asked students to define a key concept in qualitative research. To receive the maximum score, students had to provide an accurate definition, elaborate on it using course materials, and contextualize it within qualitative research. The second task assessed students' ability to apply a qualitative analysis method to a short dataset. High-scoring responses included an appropriate research question, a description of the selected method, a clear account of the analytical process (coding and theme development), and a coherent interpretation of findings. The third task required students to evaluate the methodological and ethical aspects of a research setting. Full credit required identifying strengths and limitations in relation to research questions, data collection, analysis, and ethics. Emphasis was placed on internal consistency, that is, recognizing how individual design choices combine into a coherent qualitative approach. The study used authentic course data, meaning that assessment was conducted by the course instructor as part of the normal course process, and the research began only after grading had been completed. Consequently, inter-rater reliability was not calculated. However, the use of a structured rubric and the re-evaluation of a subset of responses supported consistency in grading. Students received information about the research via the course page and email, and those who declined participation were excluded. The study complied with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, 2016/679) and the Finnish Data Protection Act (1050/2018). All data were pseudonymized prior to analysis. The dataset includes home exam materials from 413 students in 2023 and 478 students in 2024 (total N = 891). We used five types of data: exam answers, platform log data, exam results, self-reported AI use, and course feedback (Table 1 ). Each dataset served a distinct role within a mixed-methods design. Exam answers, self-reports, and feedback formed the basis for qualitative analysis of AI use, while performance (points and grades) and log data (completion time) supported quantitative analysis of outcomes and efficiency. After course completion, we compiled all exam data into a spreadsheet containing exam year, submission time, task scores, total points, final grade, and self-reported AI use. Anonymous course feedback was not linked to individual students and was analyzed separately. The qualitative analysis focused on exams in which students reported AI use. We conducted a thematic analysis to identify patterns in AI use (Braun & Clarke, 2021) . The coding proceeded in four steps: 1) inductive coding of self-reports, 2) identification of recurring patterns, 3) deductive coding of exam responses with cross-validation to self-reports based on created criteria, and 4) deductive coding of course feedback. We identified three modes of AI use: instrumental, ideational, and reflective. In self-reports students described instrumental use as editing or directly adapting AI-generated text, ideational use as using AI for idea generation, and reflective use as evaluating their writing with AI tools. The first author conducted the initial inductive coding, after which the third author reviewed coding. Rather than conducting independent blind coding, the review process focused on evaluating the conceptual coherence of the categories, discussing ambiguous cases, and refining category boundaries. Particular attention was given to distinctions between instrumental and ideational use, which were less clearly differentiated than reflective use. Specifically, some students used AI primarily for improving language, grammar, or structure while leaving the substantive content largely unchanged. After discussion, these cases were classified as instrumental use because AI functioned mainly as an editing tool rather than as a source of ideas or reflective feedback. Because many self-reports were brief, we developed additional classification criteria (typical indicators) to support the following deductive coding. To refine these criteria, we compared a sample of student responses from each mode with example answers generated by ChatGPT 3.5, which was used by 85% of the students, and with established indicators of AI-generated text (Simon, 2023) . We focused on three dimensions: 1) content (superficial analysis, contextual misalignment, generic responses and factual inconsistencies in relation to course materials), 2) structure (formulaic organization, weak logical connections, mechanical use of transitions, and similar structural patterns across task types), and 3) style (overly formal tone, overly polished appearance, generic or vague wording, repetitiveness, lack of personal voice). Instrumental use was coded when AI-generated content formed the primary basis of the response with minimal modification. Ideational use was coded when AI outputs were selectively integrated into student-authored text. Reflective use was coded when AI was used primarily to refine students' own responses. In ambiguous cases, classification was based on the dominant pattern across content, structure, and style indicators. Together, we used these steps to develop the coding scheme (Appendix 1). In the final stage of qualitative analysis, by using a coding scheme, we deductively coded exam responses and open-ended course feedback. We then added AI modes to the spreadsheet, coding each exam response as non-use, instrumental, ideational, or reflective. Because AI use varied across tasks (Table 2 ), analyses were conducted at the task level, with each task treated as an independent observation. Where aggregated performance measures were used, these were calculated by combining task-level scores. We then conducted quantitative analysis by linking modes of AI use to performance (points and grades) and efficiency (completion time). First, the quantitative analysis focused on differences in results between students who used AI and those who did not. The differences were studied using a non-parametric U test due to unequal group sizes and non-normal distribution of scores. To study the possible differences in exam results between students in different modes of AI, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used. The quantitative part of the study was conducted using Jamovi software. In this dataset, insights into self-regulated learning are drawn from materials produced in an authentic course context rather than from students' explicit reflections on their learning. Within the SRL framework, the decision to use AI as a resource (and for which tasks) was interpreted as part of the forethought phase. Exam performance reflected the performance phase, and self-reports represented selfreflection. Course feedback further illuminated metacognitive reflections and motivational and emotional aspects across all phases. At the same time, reporting requirements encouraged students to monitor and reflect on their own practices. We present
analysis.discussion: Our findings suggest a gradual normalization of AI use in academic settings, reflected in increased uptake and more positive attitudes, aligning with prior research indicating generally neutral or positive student perceptions of AI in education (Ardelean & Edit, 2023; Jinchuña Huallpa et al., 2023) . However, ethical concerns persisted, particularly regarding whether AI-assisted exam work constitutes genuine learning. Similar student concerns have been identified in contexts AI use may compromise fairness and skill development (Chaudhry et al., 2023) . Overall, the findings challenge the notion of students as uniform adopters of AI. Instead, attitudes and emotions toward AI differ, shaping how and whether students use LLMs in academic tasks. This variation underlines the need for more nuanced, context-sensitive accounts of AI use in authentic learning situations. This study shows that students' use of AI in academic tasks is not uniform but varies in meaningful ways. We identified three modes of AI use-instrumental, ideational, and reflective-and found that these are associated with different levels of engagement and performance. Students who engaged more evaluatively with AI tended to demonstrate stronger and more consistent outcomes, while more instrumental use was sometimes associated with weaker performance, especially in tasks requiring contextualization and critical interpretation. Taken together, these findings indicate that the role of AI in learning depends on how students use it. AI is not inherently beneficial or harmful; rather, its effects depend on how students regulate its use. In this sense, AI makes students' self-regulatory capacities more visible and potentially more consequential. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing the skills needed to use AI thoughtfully and critically, so that it contributes to meaningful learning rather than mere task completion.
analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. First, the data were collected during the early stages of widespread generative AI adoption, when many students were still experimenting with the technology. As a result, the proposed categorization of AI use should be considered an initial framework, open to further refinement. In addition, the study was conducted in the context of home exams, which represent a specific assessment setting. Comparisons to more complex academic tasks, such as thesis writing, should therefore be made with caution, as students may employ multiple AI strategies across extended projects and use a wider range of tools. Second, the study is based on naturally occurring data without experimental control. Consequently, self-regulated learning processes were inferred rather than directly measured. The analysis relies primarily on self-reports, which varied in detail and did not include prompts, limiting insight into actual AI interactions. This may have affected the classification of AI use, particularly in distinguishing between ideational and reflective modes. In addition, it is possible that some students did not disclose their AI use, which could lead to under-or overestimation of differences between groups. As AI models evolved rapidly during data collection (2023-2024), differences in tool capabilities may have influenced the effectiveness of certain usage strategies. And variation in exam tasks across sessions may also affect comparability, despite the use of a shared grading rubric. A further limitation concerns interpretation. As an observational and mainly qualitative study, the findings indicate associations rather than causal relationships. In particular, students who engaged in more evaluative or reflective forms of AI use may already have differed from others in terms of prior ability, motivation, or self-regulatory capacity. This makes it difficult to disentangle whether differences in performance are related to AI use itself or to underlying student characteristics. The study is also limited by its theoretical framing. Although selfregulated learning provided a useful framework for identifying differences in students' AI use, the aim was not to measure or validate SRL processes as such. Consequently, the findings primarily, and somewhat simplistically, draw attention to students' self-regulation in integrating AI as a learning resource. Alternative theoretical perspectives, such as deep learning or digital literacy, might have provided greater insight into the learning processes themselves or the critical skills required to use AI tools. Both of these aspects deserve further exploration. Thus, the study provides only partial access to students' learning processes. While self-reports and feedback offer useful insights, they do not capture students' internal motivations, planning strategies, or realtime decision-making. In particular, motivational factors such as task value, goal orientation, and self-efficacy were not directly measured, even though the findings suggest they play an important role in shaping AI use. Given the complexity of motivation as a research domain, future studies would benefit from employing methods specifically designed to capture these dimensions more systematically. The findings cannot be generalized statistically to all higher education contexts where students use generative AI for written assignments. The study is based on an authentic teaching situation, with all its inherent imperfections, and it began as a qualitative and conceptual process to which quantitative elements were added later on. The findings should therefore be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive. However, the consistency of the identified patterns across two academic years suggests that the distinction between instrumental, ideational, and reflective AI use may have relevance beyond the specific course examined here. Despite these limitations, the study highlights the complex and nonuniform role of AI in educational settings. Drawing on authentic assessment context, longitudinal design spanning two academic years, and triangulated data, the study provides a robust account of how students engage with AI in practice. The findings suggest that the pedagogical value of AI depends less on the tool itself and more on how students regulate its use within learning processes. The findings may inform educational decision-making in several ways. First, they suggest that educational interventions should focus not only on whether students use AI, but also on how they use it. Second, instruction on AI literacy should emphasize critical evaluation, adaptation, and reflection rather than task completion. Third, assessment practices may benefit from rewarding contextualization, critical thinking, and reflective engagement, which appear to distinguish higher-performing forms of AI use. Future research should examine how instructional approaches and targeted support can help students engage with AI in ways that sustain autonomy, critical thinking, and deep learning.

preview: This study examined students’ AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, and ethical awareness following participation in a structured, AI-integrated classroom activity.
