abstract_text: This study examined students’ AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, and ethical awareness following participation in a structured, AI-integrated classroom activity. The study also investigated the relationships among these constructs and examined whether perceived learning benefits mediate the relationship between AI literacy and ethical awareness. In addition, the study explored whether students’ responses differed according to gender, prior AI experience, and frequency of AI use. The study involved 104 undergraduate students who participated in a hands-on classroom activity over two academic semesters. Students used generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, to prepare and deliver short lessons to their classmates, followed by discussions addressing responsible and ethical AI use. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, ethical awareness, and related aspects of students’ experiences. Overall, students reported positive perceptions of the learning experience. They strongly agreed that AI made learning easier and more enjoyable (M = 4.29), saved time on academic tasks (M = 4.27), and helped improve the quality of their work (M = 4.09). AI literacy was positively correlated with perceived learning benefits (r = 0.559, p .05). The findings suggest that students’ AI literacy is associated with greater perceived learning benefits and ethical awareness. Furthermore, the study examines the potential mediating role of perceived learning benefits in the relationship between AI literacy and ethical awareness. These findings highlight the importance of structured, meaningful classroom activities that encourage students to actively engage with, evaluate, and take responsibility for AI-generated content rather than relying on AI outputs passively.

As presented in Table 4 , participants reported high levels across all three domains. AI Literacy scored (W.A = 3.81, SD = 0.908), with the highest-rated item being understanding how AI assists in lesson preparation (W.A = 4.01), followed by critical thinking about AI-generated content (W.A = 3.84), and active engagement (W.A = 3.56). Perceived Benefits scored very high (W.A = 4.215, SD = 0.874). Students rated "AI made learning easier and more enjoyable" highest (W.A = 4.288), followed by time savings (W.A = 4.269), and improved quality of work (W.A = 4.087). Ethical Awareness scored high (W.A = 4.103, SD = 0.846). The highest-rated item was commitment to responsible AI use (W.A = 4.279), followed by understanding ethical use after the activity (W.A = 4.183), and support for institutional guidelines (W.A = 4.067). Chi-square Goodness-of-Fit tests confirmed significant deviations from uniform distribution across all domains ( p < .001). Combined with the one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test results reported above, these findings indicate that students demonstrated a positive directional consensus in their responses, consistently above the neutral midpoint. For the mediation analysis, a bootstrapping procedure (5,000 samples) was used, as it is robust against violations of normality assumptions. To examine the mediating role of Perceived Benefits (M) in the association between AI Literacy (X) and Ethical Awareness (Y), Hayes' PROCESS Macro (Model 4) was utilized with 5,000 bootstrap samples. The results revealed the following: Path A (X → M): AI Literacy was significantly and positively associated with Perceived Benefits (β = 0.538, p < .001), explaining 31.2% of its variance. Path B (M → Y): Perceived Benefits was significantly and positively associated with Ethical Awareness (β = 0.360, p < .001), after controlling for AI Literacy. Direct association (X → Y): The direct association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness was not statistically significant after accounting for Perceived Benefits (β = 0.165, p = .091). Indirect effect (X → M → Y): The indirect effect was statistically significant (Effect = 0.194, BootLLCI = 0.051, BootULCI = 0.361). Because the bootstrap confidence interval does not include zero, the results provide evidence consistent with an indirect mediation pathway. The results showed that after the AI activity, students had good AI literacy (M = 3.81), very good perceived benefits (M = 4.22), and good ethical awareness (M = 4.10). Students said that AI helped them save time (71.2%), improved their ability to solve problems (71.2%), and strengthened their critical thinking (62.5%). At the same time, some students worried about incorrect AI outputs (54.8%) and plagiarism (35.0%). This shows that students have a balanced and thoughtful view of AI tools. The statistical analysis also showed that students who had used AI before the activity had higher perceived benefits (p = .003) and higher ethical awareness (p = .005). However, gender and academic level did not make any difference in the results. Also, how often students used AI was linked to all three areas (p < .01). This means that using AI more often helps students build better skills and awareness.
analysis.discussion: The results indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness through Perceived Benefits, while the direct association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness was not statistically significant. These findings are consistent with the interpretation that the association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness may operate indirectly through Perceived Benefits. However, given the cross-sectional design, these findings are correlational and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal pathway. Higher levels of perceived AI Literacy were associated with higher Perceived Benefits, which were in turn associated with higher Ethical Awareness. The aim of this study was to analyze the influence of the class activity based on the application of generative AI on the AI literacy, learning benefits perceived by undergraduate students, and their ethical awareness. The findings have shown a statistically significant indirect effect of the AI literacy on the ethical awareness via the perception of learning benefits, as hypothesized in the proposed theory. This relationship is in line with-but does not prove-the possible process through which AI literacy is associated with the perception of the usefulness of AI, which is further associated with perceived learning benefits (savings in time, improvement in quality, pleasure) and, finally, with ethical awareness. This finding aligns with Self-Determination Theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000) . When students experience competence through perceived benefits, they are more likely to internalize responsible behaviors. It also supports Expectancy-Value Theory (Eccles and Wigfield, 2002) , where value beliefs (perceived benefits) mediate the relationship between competence beliefs (AI literacy) and behavioral outcomes (ethical awareness). Notably, the insignificant direct effect (β = 0.165, p = .091) together with the significant indirect effect suggests that AI literacy does not have a direct association with ethical awareness when learning gains are controlled for. This implies several important implications for teaching practice: instructors must not rely on the belief that the mere teaching of AI techniques fosters responsible conduct. Students must also experience and value the benefits of AI use.
analysis.limitations: • First, the sample (N = 104) came from only one university, and students were chosen based on convenience. This means the results may not apply to all students. • Second, the study used self-reported answers, which may not be completely accurate (common method bias; Podsakoff et al., 2003) because students might answer in a way they think looks good. • Third, there was no control group, so we cannot say for sure that the activity caused the results. • Fourth, the study measured outcomes right after the activity. We need follow-up studies to see if the gains in literacy, benefits, and awareness last over time, • Fifth, although the study included open-ended questions, a systematic qualitative analysis was not conducted. Therefore, the study should be characterized as predominantly quantitative, with qualitative data used for exploratory purposes only. Future research should employ rigorous qualitative methods such as thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) or in-depth interviews to capture richer insights into students' experiences, • Sixth, the study's findings are based on self-reported data, which may be subject to social desirability bias or inaccurate recall. Future studies should incorporate objective measures of student performance and AI interaction behaviors (Podsakoff et al., 2003) .

abstract_text: The call for papers for the 2025 PESA conference referenced our ‘increasingly pluralistic, post-truth, post-reality and divided world’ and the ‘existential problems’ that we face—noting climate change, AI, populism and the decline in ethical and reasoned discourse. The assumption contained in the call was that equipping young people with the ability to engage in reasoned deliberation is more pressing than ever before. And certainly, educating for critical thinking—thoughtfulness, coherence, rationality—is often held up as a silver bullet to heal our seemingly ailing and divided world. Perhaps rightly so. But here, I apply some critical thinking to the claim. Drawing on many years of involvement in teaching philosophy and ethics at the tertiary level, I reflect on what teaching critical thinking skills can, and cannot, achieve. I question the pervasive ‘crisis’ framing in education, suggesting that constant existential rhetoric can leave students anxious and less resilient and I argue for some guiding principles: teach students how to think, not what to think; and guard against ideological narrowing, ensuring critical thinking is genuinely open to diverse perspectives, including those that make us uncomfortable. Rather than a cure-all, critical thinking should be taught as a discipline grounded in humility, charity, and the courage to engage with difference. Its power lies not in solving every societal problem, but in equipping students to reason together in good faith—even when the stakes are existential.

analysis.methods: The study used a cross-sectional survey design. Convenience sampling was used to administer paper-and-pencil questionnaires to undergraduate students at universities in mainland China during the 2024–2025 academic year. After data screening for completeness and inattentive responding, 421 valid questionnaires were retained for analysis. Of these participants, 128 (30.4%) identified as male and 293 (69.6%) as female. The sample comprised 116 first-year (27.6%), 101 second-year (24.0%), 164 third-year (39.0%) and 40 fourth-year (9.5%) students, drawn from a range of disciplines. The sample size comfortably exceeds the minimum required for PLS-SEM with the present model complexity, satisfying both Cohen’s power conventions and the inverse-square-root rule ( Hair et al., 2021 ; Kock and Hadaya, 2018 ). All participation was voluntary and anonymous. Before completing the questionnaire, students were informed of the study purpose and the protections in place; they gave written informed consent and were assured that responses would be used solely for academic research and that they could withdraw at any time. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the authors’ institution and approved by the relevant Institutional Review Board. To reduce potential common method bias, the questionnaire was pilot-tested on 30 undergraduates not included in the final sample, items were arranged so that the predictor and criterion measures were separated, and procedural remedies recommended by Podsakoff et al. (2003) were applied (e.g., guaranteed anonymity, balanced item polarity, and clear instructions emphasising that there were no right or wrong answers). All scales were administered in Chinese; English-language scales were translated and back-translated by two bilingual researchers, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer and the wording revised after a small-scale pilot. Items were rated on a five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) unless otherwise noted. Scale scores reported in Table 1 were calculated as the sum of the constituent items, with higher scores indicating higher levels of the construct; for the PLS-SEM measurement model, dimension and parcel scores were computed as item means (Section 3.3), which is immaterial for estimation because PLS-SEM standardises all indicators. Means, standard deviations and zero-order correlations. GenAI use was measured with the 17-item College Students’ Generative AI Use Survey developed by Li et al. (2024) . The instrument captures students’ use of GenAI across four typical scenarios identified through literature review and semi-structured interviews with undergraduates: course learning, research activities, daily life, and further-study and job seeking. Sample items include “I use generative AI to answer the questions my teachers ask in class”, “I use generative AI to assist me in selecting research questions”, “When I encounter difficulties in life (such as diet, financial management or social relationships), I turn to generative AI for help”, and “I ask generative AI to help me create or revise my résumé”. The scale has demonstrated acceptable reliability in prior Chinese university samples. The critical-thinking outcome was operationalised as self-reported critical analytical skills using the eight-item Critical Analytical Skills sub-scale of Hou et al.’s (2022) Chinese Critical Thinking Scale. The sub-scale assesses individuals’ perceived ability to systematically gather and analyse problem-relevant background information and evaluate its veracity. Sample items include “I prefer to follow a structured set of steps when solving problems”, “I often consider the views of my parents and elders when making decisions”, and “I make different decisions in different situations when faced with a problem”. The Chinese Critical Thinking Scale was developed and validated specifically for Chinese university samples and has demonstrated good psychometric properties; higher scores indicate stronger self-reported critical analytical skills. Following the item-to-construct balance approach ( Little et al., 2002 ), the eight items were aggregated into three parcels for use as indicators of the latent critical analytical skills construct. Specifically, the items were first ranked according to their standardised factor loadings, and relatively higher- and lower-loading items were systematically distributed across the three parcels to balance their relationships with the underlying construct. Parcel scores were calculated as the mean of their constituent items. The resulting three parcels, labelled CT Parcel 1, CT Parcel 2, and CT Parcel 3, were specified as reflective indicators of a single latent critical analytical skills construct. They therefore represent aggregated measurement indicators rather than theoretically distinct dimensions of critical thinking ( Little et al., 2002 ; Matsunaga, 2008 ). GenAI feedback literacy was assessed using the 39-item Generative AI Student Feedback Literacy Scale (GenAI-SFLS) developed and validated for Chinese college students by Cui et al. (2026) . The instrument is organised around four dimensions and nine specific factors: a cognitive dimension (feedback knowledge and feedback appreciation); a behavioural dimension (feedback prompting skills, feedback judgement and enaction of feedback); an affective dimension (emotional recognition, readiness to engage and commitment to change); and an ethical dimension (feedback ethics). The four-dimension architecture extends Carless and Boud’s (2018) general feedback-literacy framework to AI-mediated environments, where prompt engineering and ethical engagement become central to the construct ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Zhan and Yan, 2026 ). Reflective thinking was measured with the Reflective Thinking Scale (RTS) developed by Kember et al. (2000) , one of the most widely used instruments in this area; in the present study, the Chinese-context revised version validated by Fu and Hali (2025) for use with students in mainland Chinese universities was adopted. The RTS captures four dimensions on a continuum of reflection: habitual action, understanding, reflection and critical reflection, with habitual action representing the least reflective level and critical reflection the most advanced. A sample item is “I often re-appraise my experience so I can learn from it and improve for my next performance”. Items were rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = definitely disagree, 5 = definitely agree). The four-factor structure has shown good reliability and construct validity in Chinese university samples ( Fu and Hali, 2025 ; Kember et al., 2000 ). The analysis proceeded in two stages. analysis.results: To evaluate the discriminant validity of the four study constructs, a series of nested confirmatory factor analyses was conducted in AMOS 26.0 with maximum likelihood estimation ( Table 3 ). The four-factor model best represented the underlying factor structure (χ 2 /df = 2.189; CFI = 0.731; TLI = 0.723; IFI = 0.732; RMSEA = 0.053), with all factor loadings statistically significant. Although the incremental fit indices (CFI, TLI and IFI) fall below conventional thresholds (a well-documented consequence of model size: incremental fit indices such as CFI and TLI decline as the number of indicators per factor increases, even when RMSEA remains acceptable, and the present item-level model comprises 80 indicators, 39 of them from the GenAI-SFLS; Kenny and McCoach, 2003 ; Shi et al., 2019 ), the four-factor model fit was clearly superior to the three-, two- and single-factor alternatives, indicating adequate factorial differentiation amongst GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking and reflective thinking. Confirmatory factor analyses of the measurement model. N = 421; maximum likelihood estimation in AMOS 26.0. Model 2 is the hypothesised four-factor model (GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking, reflective thinking). Model 1 adds an unmeasured common method factor, on which all indicators load, to the four substantive factors. Model 3 combines critical thinking and reflective thinking into one factor; Model 4 additionally combines GenAI feedback literacy with critical thinking and reflective thinking; Model 5 loads all indicators on a single factor. Common method bias was further checked with Harman’s single-factor test ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Twenty-one factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted from the unrotated solution; the first factor accounted for only 21.46% of the variance, well below the 40% threshold. In the unmeasured method factor approach ( Tang and Wen, 2020 ), adding a common method factor to the four-factor model (Model 1 in Table 3 ) did not improve model fit (CFI 0.699 vs. 0.731; TLI 0.688 vs. 0.723), indicating that a common method factor does not account for the covariance amongst the indicators ( Wen et al., 2018 ). Both procedures suggest that common method bias is unlikely to be a serious concern in the present data. Table 1 reports means, standard deviations and zero-order correlations amongst the four study variables. GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking and reflective thinking were significantly and positively inter-correlated (all p < 0.001). The pattern is consistent with the proposed model: GenAI use is most strongly correlated with feedback literacy, and feedback literacy and reflective thinking show the strongest associations with critical thinking, anticipating their roles as mediator and moderator. Table 2 reports the indicator loadings, internal consistency (Cronbach’s α and composite reliability, CR) and convergent validity (average variance extracted, AVE) for each latent construct. All indicator loadings exceeded 0.70, supporting indicator reliability. Cronbach’s α values exceeded 0.70 ( Fornell and Larcker, 1981 ), CR values exceeded 0.80 and the more precise reliability coefficient ρA ranged from 0.769 to 0.897 ( Hair et al., 2021 ), confirming internal consistency. AVE values exceeded 0.60 ( Barclay et al., 1995 ), indicating adequate convergent validity. The square root of each construct’s AVE exceeded its correlations with the other constructs, satisfying the Fornell–Larcker criterion. Heterotrait–monotrait (HTMT) ratios across all construct pairs (0.309, 0.514, 0.583, 0.315, 0.715 and 0.546) were well below the conservative 0.85 threshold ( Henseler et al., 2016 ), supporting discriminant validity. Outer VIF values for the dimension-level indicators and parcels ranged from 1.340 to 2.670, except for the behavioural dimension of GenAI feedback literacy (VIF = 4.019), which exceeds the ideal value of 3 but remains below the critical value of 5 ( Hair et al., 2021 ); indicator collinearity is therefore not a serious concern. Following Chin’s (2009) recommendation, the structural model was estimated in SmartPLS 4.1.1.4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Path coefficients are reported in Table 4 . GenAI use significantly predicted GenAI feedback literacy ( β = 0.438, t = 8.335, p < 0.001), supporting H2. The total effect of GenAI use on critical thinking, equivalent to its estimate when modelled without the mediator, was also significant ( β = 0.257, t = 4.864, p < 0.001), supporting H1. GenAI feedback literacy significantly predicted critical thinking ( β = 0.421, t = 8.309, p < 0.001), supporting H3. analysis.discussion: This study set out to test a moderated mediation model linking generative artificial intelligence use to university students’ self-reported critical thinking, with GenAI feedback literacy as the mechanism and reflective thinking as a boundary condition. Three findings stand out. First, GenAI use was positively related to critical thinking, both directly when modelled alone and through GenAI feedback literacy when both were entered together. Second, the inclusion of feedback literacy reduced the direct effect to non-significance and accounted for nearly three-quarters of the total effect, a pattern consistent with feedback literacy as a principal mechanism. Third, the model was conditional on reflective thinking: at low reflective thinking the link was direct and the indirect path was not significant, whereas at high reflective thinking the indirect path through feedback literacy strengthened and the direct path disappeared. Read together, these results are consistent with a dual-route interpretation of the inconsistent existing evidence on GenAI and critical thinking, in which the structure of the association is sensitive to learner disposition. Each finding warrants discussion. Before turning to each finding, one interpretive boundary should be made explicit. Critical thinking was measured with the critical analytical skills sub-scale of the Chinese Critical Thinking Scale, on which students rate their own habitual analytical behaviour. The outcome therefore represents self-reported critical analytical skills, not critical-thinking performance demonstrated on a task, a test or an expert-rated piece of work. Self-reports of this kind capture students’ perceptions of how they approach problems rather than the observed quality of their reasoning, and they share a method with the self-reported predictors. Accordingly, where we write that GenAI use, feedback literacy or reflective thinking “predicts” critical thinking, the claim is that these variables are associated with higher self-rated analytical skill in a cross-sectional model, not that they produce better critical-thinking performance. This boundary applies to every finding discussed below. Generative AI is rapidly becoming part of the cognitive infrastructure of higher education, and a settled empirical answer to whether its use is associated with stronger or weaker critical thinking has remained elusive. The present study reframes the question. In a cross-sectional sample of Chinese undergraduates, GenAI use was positively associated with self-reported critical analytical skills, but the association was largely indirect: it was carried by students’ capacity to interpret, judge and act on AI-generated feedback, and its structure depended on students’ reflective stance. At low reflective thinking the association was direct and modest; at high reflective thinking it ran through feedback literacy, yielding a stronger indirect association. If these associations reflect the hypothesised causal ordering, a question that longitudinal and experimental designs must settle, the cognitive dividend of GenAI is unlikely to come from access alone, and universities that pair AI integration with explicit feedback-literacy training and reflective pedagogical practises may be better placed to convert ubiquitous AI use into the analytical capacity that higher education is meant to cultivate. The moderated mediation model presented here offers a tractable framework for the next wave of empirical work on GenAI and higher-order cognition.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations bound the study’s claims. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. All variables were measured concurrently, so the mediation and moderated-mediation estimates describe patterns of association that are consistent with the hypothesised ordering but cannot establish it; reverse or reciprocal orderings (for example, students with stronger analytical skills making heavier or more sophisticated use of GenAI, or feedback literacy shaping use rather than the reverse) are equally compatible with the data. Although PLS-SEM with bootstrapped indirect effects and theoretically motivated path direction is well suited to estimating complex models, the findings should be replicated using longitudinal panel data or randomised intervention designs that track how GenAI use, feedback literacy and reflective thinking co-evolve over time. Second, the sample is drawn from Chinese universities and is skewed female (69.6%); cross-cultural and gender-balanced replications are needed to assess generalisability across educational systems with different assessment cultures and AI-policy environments. Third, all measures are self-reported, and the outcome in particular represents self-reported critical analytical skills rather than demonstrated critical-thinking performance. Although the study’s common-method-bias diagnostics did not flag a serious problem, behavioural and performance-based measures of critical thinking and feedback engagement (e.g., analyses of think-aloud protocols, log data from AI interactions, expert ratings of student work) would strengthen inference ( Fan et al., 2025 ). Fourth, critical thinking was operationalised through the analytical-skills sub-scale of a Chinese instrument; future studies could examine the model with broader operationalisations covering inference, evaluation, explanation and self-regulation ( Facione, 2011 ) and across disciplines, since GenAI’s affordances and risks may differ between, say, the humanities and STEM. Relatedly, the dual-route interpretation in this study rests on the pattern of moderation, not on direct observation of cognitive processing; the study did not measure whether students engaged with GenAI outputs shallowly or deeply, and process-tracing methods such as interaction logs, think-aloud protocols or eye-tracking are needed to test the proposed routes directly. Fifth, the incremental fit indices of the item-level measurement model fell below conventional thresholds, as is common with long instruments such as the 39-item GenAI-SFLS ( Kenny and McCoach, 2003 ; Shi et al., 2019 ); future work could refine the GenAI-SFLS for shorter administration without losing dimensional coverage. Finally, GenAI tools are evolving rapidly, and the empirical model captures a snapshot of usage patterns at a given moment; tracking the moderated mediation structure across model generations and modalities (text, voice, multimodal agents) is an important agenda for the field.

Three findings stand out. First, GenAI use was positively related to critical thinking, both directly when modelled alone and through GenAI feedback literacy when both were entered together. Second, the inclusion of feedback literacy reduced the direct effect to non-significance and accounted for nearly three-quarters of the total effect, a pattern consistent with feedback literacy as a principal mechanism. Third, the model was conditional on reflective thinking: at low reflective thinking the link was direct and the indirect path was not significant, whereas at high reflective thinking the indirect path through feedback literacy strengthened and the direct path disappeared. Read together, these results are consistent with a dual-route interpretation of the inconsistent existing evidence on GenAI and critical thinking, in which the structure of the association is sensitive to learner disposition. title: From digital companionship to capability building: reframing conversational artificial intelligence and older adults' psychological wellbeing in active aging
preview: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. Existing research has predominantly interpreted conversational AI through the lens of digital companionship, emphasizing its capacity to simulate social presence, reduce loneliness, and provide emot…
abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. Existing research has predominantly interpreted conversational AI through the lens of digital companionship, emphasizing its capacity to simulate social presence, reduce loneliness, and provide emotional support. While this perspective captures important affective outcomes, it offers a limited account of the developmental processes through which AI engagement may influence psychological wellbeing in aging populations. This conceptual analysis proposes a shift from a companionship-oriented paradigm to a capability-building perspective grounded in the Capability Approach. It argues that the primary value of conversational AI lies not in its ability to substitute social interaction, but in its potential to expand older adults' cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capabilities. Building on this argument, this paper develops an AI-Augmented Active Aging Framework that explains how conversational AI affordances, responsiveness, personalization, accessibility, and availability, interact with personal, social, environmental, and system-level conversion factors. Under supportive conditions, these affordances may facilitate cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capability formation, thereby supporting autonomy, competence, social integration, and active aging. Under adverse conditions, however, conversational AI may contribute to capability erosion through over-reliance, cognitive offloading, reduced human contact, or diminished autonomous judgment. The framework therefore emphasizes heterogeneous and conditional outcomes rather than assuming uniform benefits across older adults.

abstract_text: The importance of critical thinking when using generative AI in personal, professional, and educational contexts is widely acknowledged by scholars, educators, and politicians. There are contradictory hypotheses regarding the influence of AI on critical thinking, and research thus far has produced mixed results. In this paper, we present a critical scoping review of 80 research papers from Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) that study critical thinking with or about AI, focusing on how “critical thinking” is defined, measured, and how the papers claim critical thinking to be influenced by AI, according to current HCI research. Our findings demonstrate that critical thinking is rarely defined in HCI research about AI, and there are fundamental construct and criterion validity challenges in this line of research. We present a research agenda for more theory-grounded empirical research in critical thinking with or about AI, based on cognitive-psychological, philosophical, or educational research traditions.

Since HCI draws on theories and methods from multiple other fields, we expect that studies published at HCI venues are likely to represent (in terms of methods and findings) findings published in other, specialized venues (such as education or psychology). The phenomenon of interest is specifically critical thinking, and a mapping of the emerging evidence in HCI about AI as a claimed influence on critical thinking. The complex and heterogeneous nature of recent findings within this theme makes it suitable for a scoping review rather than a systematic review (Peters et al., 2015) . We focuson the term critical thinking, and not on related concepts or skills, e.g., reflection in practice (Cho et al., 2022) , critical reflection (Iivari et al., 2024) , analytical thinking (Buc ¸inca et al., 2021) or stop-and-think behavior (Gauthier et al., 2022) . While these terms would be relevant if we wanted to systematically assess how AI affects critical thinking ability, this review is focused on how HCI interprets and uses the lexical term critical thinking. Critical thinking is particularly interesting because the term is commonly used across different disciplines, while related skills and behaviors often have roots in one discipline (for instance, "critical reflection" and "reflective practice" tend to be used in design research, while "analytical thinking" and "stop-and-think behavior" stem from a cognitive psychology tradition). analysis.discussion: The goal of this section is to lay out potential paths forward. We first describe the general challenges that pervade the study of critical thinking with or about AI in HCI research. We then outline some potential approaches to meet these challenges, both by looking at exemplars from the corpus, and then by revisiting the three theoretical traditions and what these might be able to offer in terms of designs of future studies. In this paper, we presented a scoping review of 80 research papers that empirically studied critical thinking in the context of using AI, a new but increasingly popular topic in HCI, and found that the included studies were highly heterogeneous in terms of their definitions of critical thinking and their studies of it. The studies are conducted especially in the USA, with students as participants, and using LLMs as the AI technology. Most of the studies evaluate a system designed to influence critical thinking, and most are based on short-term interventions and attitudinal rather than behavioral assessment. Several observations about the corpus indicate construct validity challenges, such as a lack of clear and/or shared definitions of critical thinking and how this is assessed, especially in the question of perceived versus demonstrated critical thinking. A majority of the studies in the corpus rely on selfassessment as a measure of critical thinking; in fact, self-assessment measurements account for half (25 of the total 50) of the submissions that claim that AI has a primarily positive influence on people's critical thinking ability. Of the studies that base their assessment on a demonstrated effect of AI on critical thinking specifically, only 10 submissions provide explicit and reproducible criteria for how their assessment is made. We also identified potential criterion/content validity challenges, and a notable absence of in vivostudies or studies which focus on professionals rather than students. This means that it is difficult to know whether the studies actually predict or explain the type and scope of critical thinking we may be interested in assessing. Finally, we suggested some ways forward for HCI research that attempts to evaluate the influence of AI on critical thinking, based on the three theoretical foundations of cognitive psychology, philosophy, and education. We suggest that future studies of critical thinking in the context of using AI could make even clearer contributions by making explicit, at least, what their definition of critical thinking is, how they evaluate the influence, and finally, why their chosen method can reasonably be believed to measure what it is intended to measure.
analysis.limitations: A main limitation of this review is the possibility of misrepresenting the actual body of research about "critical thinking and related concepts." Searching with keywords is inherently reductionist, and our search is likely to have missed some existing work. Because we limited our search to the specific term "critical thinking" (as opposed to related terms such as "decision-making," "critical evaluation," or "reflective thinking"), we may have excluded work using a different terminology. However, as described in the methodology, this scoping review is about critical thinking-other definitions would be a matter for different (systematic rather than scoping) reviews. A second limitation is our focus on the HCI domain and our venue-based definition of this domain. Our search was confined to the ACM Digital Library, the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, and International Journal of Human-Computer Studies as representative for HCI work. Outside these databases, there is likely HCI-work to be found. Most importantly, we have not reviewed work from psychology or education, which could topically be characterized as at least HCI-adjacent research. However, our intention with this review was to bring attention to the gaps of work conducted in the domain of HCI. We believe that because this field draws upon many psychological and educational traditions, it is important to articulate more clearly which foundations are drawn upon in individual work. A third limitation is that we did not perform any quality assessment of the articles included in the corpus. When we report "claimed influence," it should not be interpreted as evidence for proven influence. A fourth limitation is that extraction of data was performed primarily by the first author. This may have biased the judgment in cases where decisions had to be made between assigning one category or another. We deem the influence of this acceptable, considering our focus was on relatively objective categorizations and not qualitative analysis. Finally, the rapidly evolving research area makes it likely that the corpus will become outdated or misrepresentative relatively fast. We do believe our scoping review merits further systematic review of work in this area. Especially the heterogeneity of the studies in terms of use of the term "critical thinking," their divergent focus on critical thinking with/about AI, and their varying levels of detail about data used as basis for the conclusions warrant this.

title: Generative AI feedback in EFL writing instruction: a mixed-methods study on performance, motivation, and self-regulated learning
preview: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, AI feedback in EFL writing instruction has gained increasing attention. Grounded in social cognitive theory and self-regulated learning theory, this mixed-methods study compared AI-mediated and teacher-mediated feedback delivery modes and examined their relationships with writing performance, learning motivation, and self-regulated learning among 120 s…
abstract_text: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, AI feedback in EFL writing instruction has gained increasing attention. Grounded in social cognitive theory and self-regulated learning theory, this mixed-methods study compared AI-mediated and teacher-mediated feedback delivery modes and examined their relationships with writing performance, learning motivation, and self-regulated learning among 120 s-year English majors at Henan Normal University. A 16-week quasi-experimental pretest-posttest-delayed test design was combined with semi-structured interviews. Repeated measures ANOVA and mediation analysis (PROCESS macro) were used for quantitative analysis; thematic analysis was applied qualitatively. The AI-mediated feedback condition was associated with greater improvement in writing performance (group × time interaction: p < 0.001, η2p = 0.12), with the largest effect on grammatical accuracy (η2p = 0.16), higher writing self-efficacy (4.42→5.82), and reduced writing anxiety (3.95→2.78). Learning motivation and self-regulated learning positively correlated (r = 0.64, p < 0.001) and partially mediated the feedback condition to performance relationship (indirect effects: b = 0.38 and b = 0.45, respectively). Qualitative themes revealed learners’ adaptive progression from passive acceptance to critical AI usage. These findings extend feedback theory to the digital context and offer an integrated framework for AI-assisted language learning.

title: The illusion of cognitive independence in the age of generative AI: unpacking GenAI literacy and learner profiles
preview: Introduction With the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education, research attention must shift from the frequency of tool use to how these tools are used by learners. Methods Drawing on questionnaire data from a large, diverse internatio…
abstract_text: Introduction With the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education, research attention must shift from the frequency of tool use to how these tools are used by learners. This study examines how GenAI literacy is related to learners' patterns of GenAI use and cognitive engagement during GenAI interactions. Methods Drawing on questionnaire data from a large, diverse international sample of academic learners (N = 848), hierarchical multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine the relationships between dimensions of GenAI literacy and actual usage behaviors. Cluster analysis was then used to identify learner profiles based on patterns of GenAI use, literacy, monitoring, and reliance. Results The findings indicate a dual role for critical-ethical awareness, a dimension of GenAI literacy that is associated with both monitoring GenAI outputs and using GenAI as a cognitive shortcut. Cluster analysis identified three learner profiles: Engaged and Literate users, who integrate monitoring and reliance; Uncritical Reliant users, who show high reliance but limited monitoring; and Skeptical Minimal users, who have low GenAI use but high reliance when they do engage. These patterns point to an “illusion of cognitive independence,” in which learners report high levels of independent thinking while engaging in cognitive offloading by relying on GenAI outputs without sufficient monitoring, particularly among Uncritical Reliant users. Discussion Collectively, these findings suggest that GenAI literacy does not necessarily reduce reliance on GenAI but instead shapes how learners combine monitoring with reliance. Conceptually, this positions GenAI literacy as a regulatory mechanism of human–AI interaction, extending self-regulated learning to contexts in which cognitive processes are distributed between learners and systems. These results highlight the importance of developing GenAI literacy as a practice of reflective and regulated use rather than focusing solely on increasing technology adoption.

analysis.methods: Data were collected through an online survey administered via the Prolific online research platform ( https://www.prolific.com/ ), a widely used tool for participant recruitment in behavioral and social science research. To ensure the sample comprised genuine academic learners with sufficient experience with academic learning environments, participants were required to hold a minimum educational level equivalent to a community or technical college degree, up to doctoral-level education. 3. Participants were required to be between 18 and 50 years of age. The inclusion criteria were established to encompass the population of post-secondary learners, that is, individuals who have completed high school education and continue to engage in formal or informal learning contexts. A total of 972 participants initiated the survey on the Prolific platform. After accounting for participant dropout and incomplete submissions, the final baseline sample comprised 848 participants who completed the survey's core components. Due to occasional item-level missing data, the exact sample size varies slightly across specific statistical analyses, typically ranging from N = 817 to N = 823. To preserve statistical power and sample representativeness, participants with partial item-level missing data were retained, and analysis-specific deletion was applied rather than strict listwise deletion across the entire dataset. The specific sample size for each analysis is explicitly reported in the corresponding Results sections. Importantly, prior experience with GenAI was not defined as an inclusion criterion; instead, participants' actual GenAI use frequency was measured within the survey on an 8-point scale (ranging from "None" to "Several times a day") to ensure accurate measurement of usage frequency. Participants who reported no use of GenAI (n = 38) were excluded from subsequent analyses, as they could not provide meaningful responses regarding usage behaviors. Table 1 presents the demographic and academic characteristics of the study participants. A complete country-level breakdown of the sample is provided in Supplementary Appendix B. To explore potential demographic variations within the sample, independent-samples t-tests were conducted across gender and educational levels. Consistent with recent literature highlighting gender gaps in AI perceptions and use (Otis et al., 2024; Russo et al., 2025) , significant gender differences emerged across several dimensions. Male participants reported a higher frequency of GenAI use, t(835) = 4.32, p < .001, d = 0.30; greater AI reliance, t(823) = 2.95, p = .003, d = 0.21; higher AI operational literacy, t(819) = 3.74, p < .001, d = 0.26; and higher conceptual AI knowledge, t(817) = 3.75, p < .001, d = 0.26. In contrast, female participants reported higher critical AI literacy, t(819) = 3.26, p = .001, d = 0.23; higher AI critical monitoring, t (824) = 1.98, p = .049, d = 0.14; and greater AI shortcut reliance, t (820) = 2.69, p = .007, d = 0.19. Although statistically significant, all observed gender differences were small in magnitude (ds ranging from 0.14 to 0.30). Furthermore, to examine the influence of educational level, early-stage undergraduate students (Years 1-2) were compared with more advanced students (Years 3 and above, including graduate students). No significant differences emerged across any of the measured GenAI variables (all ps > .24), with uniformly negligible effect sizes (|d| < 0.10). This indicates that while gender is associated with distinct patterns of GenAI use and literacy, the observed behaviors and perceptions remain highly consistent across different stages of academic education. To address RQ2, a cluster analysis was conducted to identify distinct profiles of academic learners based on GenAI use frequency, GenAI literacy dimensions, and GenAI reliance. To determine the optimal number of clusters, both the silhouette coefficient and the elbow method were evaluated. While the silhouette coefficient was highest for the two-cluster solution (0.225), it decreased only modestly for the three-cluster solution (0.206). Inspection of the elbow plot suggested that a three-cluster solution provided a reasonable balance between parsimony and explanatory richness, yielding conceptually distinct and interpretable profiles. Furthermore, to examine cluster stability, the sample was randomly split into two equal subsamples, and the k-means procedure was repeated independently. The three-cluster solution was successfully replicated across both subsamples, yielding highly similar cluster sizes and centroid profiles. The proportion of explained variance was nearly identical across the subsamples (R 2 = .381 and .378), confirming the robust stability of the identified cluster structure. The descriptive statistics for the clusters, along with their corresponding usage behaviors and skill outcomes, are presented in Table 4 , and the standardized cluster profiles are illustrated in Figure 1 . As noted, three distinct learner profiles emerged: Cluster 1 (n = 355) -Engaged and Literate GenAI Users: High levels of GenAI use and high levels of operational and conceptual literacy, alongside moderate levels of criticalethical awareness and reliance. Cluster 2 (n = 244) -Uncritical Reliant Users: Moderate GenAI use and reliance but low levels of critical and conceptual literacy and only moderate operational skills. Cluster 3 (n = 224) -Skeptical Minimal Users: Very low GenAI use and low reliance, alongside moderate criticalethical awareness and generally lower operational and conceptual literacy. Overall, the cluster profiles reveal meaningful heterogeneity in learners' engagement with GenAI, distinguishing between highly engaged and skilled users, reliance-driven users with limited critical-ethical awareness, and low-use but relatively more skeptical learners. To further characterize the identified profiles, demographic differences across clusters were examined. Significant associations emerged for both gender and field of study. Cluster membership differed by gender, x 2 ( 2, N = 814) = 27.10, p < .001, with the Engaged & Literate profile including a higher proportion of male participants, whereas the Skeptical Minimal profile included a higher proportion of female participants. Cluster membership also varied significantly across fields of study, x 2 (10, N = 816) = 54.20, p < .001. In particular, students from engineering and exact sciences were overrepresented in the Engaged & Literate profile, whereas students from the humanities were more prevalent in the Skeptical Minimal profile. No significant differences were found for educational level, x 2 (4, N = 817) = 4.93, p = .295, age, Welch's F(2, 498) = 0.78, p = .460, or year of study, x 2 (2) = 5.56, p = .062. analysis.discussion: By adopting a process-oriented perspective, this study shifts the analytical focus from whether GenAI benefits learning to how GenAI literacy functions as a central behavioral mechanism that shapes GenAI's impact on learning processes and outcomes. Drawing on a large and diverse international sample of academic learners, the findings capture patterns of GenAI use across varied contexts and demonstrate how GenAI literacy is associated with immediate usage behaviors and academic outcomes, providing empirical support for this framework and offering several theoretical insights.
analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. The reliance on selfreported data may not fully capture learners' actual cognitive processes or accurately reflect the extent to which cognitive effort is delegated to GenAI. This is particularly relevant to the interpretation of the illusion of cognitive independence, as both perceived independence and reported behaviors were based on self-assessment rather than direct observation. In addition, as the data were collected at a single point in time, the study does not permit an examination of how GenAI literacy, interaction patterns, and learning outcomes influence one another over time or a determination of the direction of these relationships. The study also did not differentiate between types of GenAI tools or task characteristics, which may involve different levels of cognitive engagement and reliance. Furthermore, we explicitly acknowledge that the regression model predicting GenAI shortcut reliance explained a relatively small proportion of variance (R² = 7.8%). This suggests that shortcut reliance is likely shaped not only by learners' GenAI literacy but also by unmeasured moderators and contextual factors. Specifically, variables such as the type of academic task and the specific functionalities of the AI tool used may play an important role in these behaviors. To advance this line of research, future studies should move beyond self-reports and incorporate longitudinal designs or objective behavioral data, such as logging the actual edits learners make to AI-generated drafts, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the conditions and mechanisms of cognitive offloading. Another limitation concerns the sample characteristics. While the sample is internationally diverse, encompassing 36 countries, it is heavily skewed toward Southern and Eastern Europe (73%). This geographic concentration, combined with the lack of sample-size parity across countries, limits the generalizability of the findings to other cultural or educational contexts. Additionally, the age cap of 50 years established in our sampling criteria excludes mature and lifelong learners. Given that older adults may exhibit different levels of technological self-efficacy and interaction patterns, future studies should aim for a more balanced global representation and include diverse age groups to examine whether GenAI usage behaviors differ by age or cultural background. Future research could also examine the illusion of cognitive independence using behavioral and performance-based measures to better capture the gap between perceived and actual cognitive engagement. Longitudinal and experimental designs may further clarify how GenAI literacy develops over time and how it relates to changes in monitoring and reliance. longform.thesis: The authors argue that internet governance built around human users is challenged when AI agents increasingly act on people's behalf. Their concern is not simply model performance: it is the relationship between agents, accountability and the ability of people to direct actions taken for them.
longform.reasoning: The authors distinguish an agent's technical capability from the authority it legitimately exercises. Traditional Internet governance tends to focus on identities and network standards; AI governance tends to focus on model behavior. Neither alone answers who approved a particular action, for how long, or whether it can be audited and reversed.
longform.examples: They place existing authorization work, including tool-access protocols, agent-to-agent interoperability, and proposals for verifiable delegation, within a broader need for an Internet authority layer. The principal–agent relationship is their organizing analogy.
longform.tension: More autonomy can reduce friction for users while increasing the distance between a person's intention and the actions attributed to that person. Technical authorization may prove that a system had permission without establishing that its action reflected informed preferences.
longform.implications: For an attention assistant, permissions could be scoped to specific tasks and easy to revoke. A person should be able to distinguish a suggestion from an action the system has already taken, inspect delegated decisions and reverse them where possible.
longform.open_question: What evidence would show that people understand, can inspect, and can revoke the decisions an attention assistant makes for them?

title: Between Co-Intelligence and Cognitive Offloading: Educators’ Perspectives from Dutch Academic Medical Settings on Generative AI, Critical Thinking, and Adult Professional Learning
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming embedded in adult professional education, yet its capacity to accelerate academic work may also remove cognitive processes that underpin professional judgement. abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming embedded in adult professional education, yet its capacity to accelerate academic work may also remove cognitive processes that underpin professional judgement. This qualitative study explored how educators working in Dutch academic medical settings perceive GenAI’s implications for students’ critical thinking and how they believe it should be integrated into medical curricula. Seventeen educators from Dutch academic medical settings participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed thematically using a mixed inductive–deductive approach informed by the Technology Acceptance Model and the Paul–Elder critical thinking framework. Three themes were identified: educational value and efficiency; threats to independent critical thinking; and conditions for responsible integration. Educators valued GenAI for personalised learning, writing support, research assistance, accessibility, simulation, and administrative efficiency. However, they associated low-friction use with cognitive offloading, weaker source appraisal, reduced information filtering, possible erosion of foundational knowledge, and difficulties verifying authentic student understanding. Participants proposed AI literacy, transparent use, institutionally governed models, comparative human–AI tasks, simulation, staged access, and AI-free oral or in-class assessment. The findings suggest that adult professional education should design GenAI as co-intelligence rather than cognitive substitution, preserving productive friction while verifying unassisted competence.

analysis.methods: An exploratory qualitative design was used because the study addressed an emerging and context-dependent educational phenomenon and sought to understand the reasoning https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16091470 underlying educators' decisions rather than estimate prevalence (Hunter et al., 2019) . Individual semi-structured interviews enabled consistent exploration of common topics while allowing follow-up questions when participants introduced unexpected examples or distinctions (DeJonckheere & Vaughn, 2019) . The setting was Dutch undergraduate and postgraduate medical education, including educators working in academic medical centres and related medical teaching roles. The research process comprised a targeted literature review, development of the research questions and theoretical framework, design of the interview guide, participant recruitment, semi-structured interviews, transcription and verification, and thematic analysis. The interview guide (Supplementary Materials S1) was explicitly informed by TAM and the Paul-Elder framework while retaining open questions about practices, concerns, and possible curriculum responses. Seventeen medical educators participated. The sample included 11 clinician-educators and six educators or researchers with PhD-level or specialist expertise relevant to medical or health education. Participants represented several Dutch academic medical settings, although the sample was concentrated at Erasmus MC; the source participant overview also includes Amsterdam AMC, UMC Groningen, UMC Utrecht, and one dual Erasmus MC/LUMC appointment. Participants taught bachelor's, master's, or both levels of medical education. Reported teaching experience ranged from 4 to 20 years among those for whom a figure was available. Recruitment combined purposive and snowball sampling (Ahmad & Wilkins, 2025) . Initial invitations were distributed through education offices and secretariats of major Dutch academic medical centres. Four participants were recruited through the initial call; additional participants were recruited through professional referrals and medical graduate networks. Recruitment sought educators with substantial experience of medical teaching and first-hand exposure to the pedagogical changes associated with students' GenAI use. Table 1 below illustrates the sample and data collection characteristics. Sample adequacy was considered iteratively during data collection and analysis rather than being determined solely by a predetermined numerical target. As interviewing progressed, participant accounts increasingly reiterated issues that had already emerged concerning GenAI use, cognitive offloading, critical-thinking development, assessment validity, AI literacy, and curriculum responses. Towards the 15th interview, no substantively new themes relevant to the research questions were identified, and the researchers therefore judged that informational/thematic saturation had been reached within the scope of the study (Saunders et al., 2018) . The final sample of 17 participants was retained to provide further opportunity to test the stability of the developing thematic patterns and to capture divergent perspectives where present. Interviews were conducted online and lasted approximately 45-60 min. Audio was captured as .m4a recordings using a local recording device. All participants were asked the same core questions, although the interviewer omitted redundant prompts when a topic had already arisen spontaneously and used probes to clarify reasoning or request examples. Introductory questions established participants' professional roles, teaching experience, target student population, and familiarity with GenAI. The main interview sections addressed observed student uses, transparency and assessment, perceived effects on medical case work and critical thinking, boundaries between justified and unjustified use, curriculum redesign, institutional influences, and possible uses of GenAI to challenge rather than replace student thinking. 1. Require a human first pass Ask learners to formulate an initial explanation, diagnosis, argument, or draft before consulting GenAI. Preserves ideation and provides a basis for metacognitive comparison rather than immediate substitution. Participants repeatedly described processes, such as selecting relevant information, composing an argument, considering alternatives, and explaining a clinical judgement, which are interpreted as forms of productive cognitive friction. Their concern was not that difficulty is intrinsically educational, but that particular forms of cognitive effort are constitutive of the intended learning outcome. This interpretation is consistent with the Paul-Elder framework, in which intellectual traits develop through repeated application of standards such as relevance, significance, clarity, and accuracy (Paul & Elder, 1999) , and with problem-centred approaches to adult professional learning (Taylor & Hamdy, 2013) . GenAI may therefore be educationally valuable when it removes incidental barriers or provides additional perspectives and feedback, but problematic when it removes the epistemic work that learners are expected to develop. The relevant design distinction is consequently between friction that can appropriately be reduced-for example, linguistic barriers-and friction that should be preserved, such as selecting and weighing evidence in clinical reasoning. The data indicate that responsible integration cannot be delegated to individual students. Educators themselves reported uncertainty and a sense that curriculum development was lagging behind technological change. AI literacy programmes should therefore include staff as well as students, address discipline-specific risks, and be updated iteratively. Core content identified by participants includes model limitations, hallucinations, source verification, prompt design, privacy and copyright, bias, equity, and the relationship between AI output and disciplinary evidence. Institutionally governed models may be valuable where privacy, standardisation, or equitable access are priorities. Participants' examples of university-hosted or restricted LLMs illustrate one way to combine governance with pedagogical design: a model can be configured to act as a Socratic tutor, disclose information progressively, or limit data exposure. Such infrastructure does not solve the pedagogical problem by itself, but it gives institutions greater control over the conditions under which human-AI interaction occurs. analysis.discussion: This study examined the perspectives of educators working across Dutch academic medical settings on GenAI at the intersection of technology adoption, critical thinking, and professional adult learning. In relation to RQ1, educators described GenAI as highly useful and easy to use but differentiated strongly between uses that augment learners' capabilities and those that substitute for intended cognitive work. In relation to RQ2, concerns centred on cognitive offloading, weaker information and source appraisal, loss of productive friction, threats to foundational knowledge, and uncertainty about assessment validity. In relation to RQ3, participants proposed AI literacy, deliberate human-AI comparison, secure institutional tools, transparent use, staged access, and assessment formats capable of verifying unaided competence. Taken together, these findings reveal a sustained ambivalence that is more analytically useful than a simple pro/anti-AI division and point towards curriculum and assessment redesign rather than either unrestricted adoption or prohibition. The medical educators participating in this study did not describe GenAI as either an educational threat or an educational solution. They described a technology whose strongest advantages, such as low-friction access to fast, polished, and personalised output, can also create mechanisms through which learning is bypassed. GenAI was valued for writing support, personalised study, accessibility, research assistance, simulation, and educator efficiency. Concerns centred on cognitive offloading, weaker source evaluation and information filtering, possible erosion of foundational knowledge and ideation, and the declining interpretability of take-home written work as evidence of individual competence. For adult professional education, the key implication is design. GenAI should be positioned as co-intelligence rather than cognitive substitution. Curricula can preserve productive friction by requiring learners to generate, explain, compare, and verify before outsourcing; they can use GenAI deliberately for dialogue, simulation, and critique; and they can retain AI-free moments where core human competence must be demonstrated. AI literacy, educator development, privacy-preserving infrastructure, equitable access, and clear governance are not peripheral support to this model, but the institutional conditions that make it possible. The goal is therefore neither prohibition nor frictionless automation, but a learning environment in which adults become capable of using AI while retaining the intellectual autonomy required to judge when, how, and whether it should be used.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations constrain interpretation. First, the original study was conducted within an approximately six-month timeframe, which placed practical constraints on re- https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16091470 cruitment and institutional representation. Nevertheless, within the recruited sample, later interviews predominantly reiterated previously identified issues and did not generate substantively new themes relevant to the research questions, supporting the judgement that informational/thematic saturation had been reached for the principal patterns reported in this study. This judgement should not, however, be interpreted as evidence of institutional or national representativeness, particularly given the concentration of participants at Erasmus MC. Second, data collection and primary coding were undertaken by one researcher. A second researcher subsequently conducted an independent analytic review of the coding framework, coded excerpts, and developed the thematic structure and participated in resolving interpretive differences. Although this process provided an additional perspective through which to challenge and refine the analysis, the study did not employ independent double-coding of the full dataset or formal interrater-reliability testing. The findings therefore remain an interpretive analysis shaped by the researchers' respective perspectives. Because participants were predominantly based at Erasmus MC, the findings should be interpreted as contextually situated accounts from educators working in selected Dutch academic medical settings rather than as representative of medical educators nationally. Future research should use more institutionally balanced samples and include students, programme directors, learning designers, AI specialists, and other stakeholders who shape curriculum policy. Most importantly, educator perceptions of cognitive offloading should be tested against behavioural and performance data. Longitudinal or quasi-experimental studies could compare students using different GenAI designs. For example, unrestricted use, human-first-pass protocols, Socratic AI tutoring, or AI-free study on retention, source evaluation, diagnostic reasoning, writing, and transfer to novel cases. Research should also examine whether GenAI can improve inclusion without creating new inequities through premium access, differential AI literacy, or privacy constraints.

abstract_text: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence into educational environments has prompted increasing interest in how AI-generated content influences student learning. This study examines the psychological pathways through which perceived usefulness of AI-generated music influences university students' learning engagement and flow experience, with attention and AI trust functioning as parallel mediators. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and cognitive load theory, the study proposes a structural model in which perceived usefulness of AI music shaped in the stylistic tradition serves as the independent variable, attention and AI trust as mediators, and learning engagement and flow as outcome variables. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 407 university students following a four-week AI music exposure protocol. Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4.0. Results confirmed that perceived usefulness significantly predicted both attention and AI trust, which in turn positively influenced learning engagement and flow. All six hypothesised direct paths and four indirect mediation paths were supported. These findings extend TAM into the AI music context and offer practical guidance for the design of AI-enhanced learning environments.

analysis.methods: This study employed a cross-sectional quantitative survey design to examine the relationships among perceived usefulness of AI-generated music, AI trust, attention, flow, and learning engagement among university students. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was adopted as the primary analytical framework, given its suitability for theory development contexts, its robustness with non-normal data distributions, and its capacity to simultaneously evaluate measurement and structural models (Hair et al., 2019) . The study was conducted in a naturalistic learning context in which participants engaged with AI-generated music produced in the stylistic tradition of Robert Schumann's Kinderszenen, Op. 15, as background music during self-directed study sessions over a four-week period. Participants were recruited from university student cohorts via online announcements and classroom mailing lists. Interested students accessed an online survey link that first presented the study information sheet and electronic informed consent form. Only participants who provided consent could proceed. To ensure the sample matched the intended learning context, participants were screened using the following criteria: (a) currently enrolled as a university student; (b) able to engage in individual study activities during the study period; (c) able to listen to audio through headphones or speakers in a quiet environment; and (d) no self-reported severe hearing impairment. A total of 407 participants were recruited in this study. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shanxi University (No. SXULL2026005). All participants provided electronic informed consent prior to completing the online questionnaire and were informed of their right to withdraw at any stage. The AI-generated music used in this study was produced using a generative AI music system trained on the stylistic features of Robert Schumann's Kinderszenen, Op. 15, including harmonic language, melodic contour, dynamic range, and tempo characteristics. Schumann's piano repertoire has been widely associated with calm affective qualities and gentle attentional engagement, making it well-suited as lowdemand background music during cognitive activities (Gooley, 2016; Perez, 2018). The AI-generated pieces preserved these calm and reflective qualities while constituting novel musical output distinct from any existing recording. Prior to participation, all students were informed that the music they would be listening to was AIgenerated, and this explicit disclosure was a deliberate design decision to enable ecologically valid measurement of AI trust and perceived usefulness. Participants were instructed to listen to approximately 30 minutes of the designated AI-generated repertoire per day, on at least five days per week, across the four-week study period. Listening was conducted either immediately before commencing a self-selected study session (priming condition) or concurrently during the first 20 minutes of the study session (concurrent condition). This flexible protocol was designed to reflect authentic student study practices while maintaining a consistent exposure dose. At the conclusion of the four-week period, participants completed the post-exposure questionnaire via an online platform.

analysis.discussion: The present study examined the pathways through which perceived usefulness of AI-generated music influences university students' learning engagement and flow, with attention and AI trust proposed as parallel mediators. The results provided support for all six hypothesised direct paths and all four mediation paths, offering a coherent account of the psychological processes through which an AI music environment shapes student learning outcomes. The finding that perceived usefulness of AI music significantly predicted both attention and AI trust is theoretically consistent with the foundational premises of TAM. Students who believe that a technology genuinely enhances their experience are more likely to approach that technology with an open and receptive orientation (Ertmer et al., 2012) . In the context of AI-generated music, this receptive orientation appears to manifest in two psychologically distinct but complementary ways. First, it is associated with heightened attentional awareness, suggesting that a positive evaluation of the music's usefulness reduces the cognitive monitoring typically associated with novel or unfamiliar auditory stimuli, freeing attentional resources for academic tasks (Merchán Sánchez-Jara et al., 2024). Second, a positive usefulness evaluation is associated with greater trust in the AI system, indicating that students who find the music beneficial are more willing to place confidence in the system and engage with it as a legitimate study aid. These two pathways together illustrate that perceived usefulness functions as a foundational psychological orientation that ramifies across both cognitive and evaluative dimensions of the learning experience. The mediating role of attention in linking perceived usefulness to learning engagement and flow aligns with the theoretical position that attentional regulation serves as the cognitive gateway through which environmental conditions influence academic involvement. When students perceive AI music as useful, they attend more mindfully to their tasks, and this sustained attentional awareness translates into both greater engagement with academic activities and greater capacity for experiential immersion. This finding is consistent with cognitive load theory, which predicts that a learning environment experienced as supportive rather than demanding will facilitate the reallocation of cognitive resources toward taskrelevant processing (Sepp et al., 2019) . The moderate strength of these mediation paths also suggests that attention is one among several mechanisms through which AI music influences learning, a conclusion supported by the parallel significance of the AI trust pathway. The mediating role of AI trust is perhaps the most theoretically novel contribution of this study. Prior research on AI acceptance has frequently treated trust as an antecedent to behavioural intention, but less attention has been paid to its role as a mediating mechanism that links technology evaluation to experiential and motivational outcomes (Shin, 2021) . The present findings imply that trust in the AI music system functions as an affective bridge between the cognitive evaluation of perceived usefulness and the experiential states of flow and learning engagement. Students who trust the AI system are more likely to allow themselves to enter states of full absorption in academic tasks, and this openness to immersion is reflected in higher flow scores. This mechanism may operate through a reduction in selfmonitoring cognition. Students who do not trust the AI music may expend cognitive resources questioning the legitimacy or quality of the auditory environment, whereas students who trust the system can direct those resources toward the learning task itself. The relatively lower R 2 values for flow compared to learning engagement warrant consideration. Flow, as a moment-to-moment experiential state, is inherently more variable and situationally sensitive than traitlike engagement orientations. The finding that perceived usefulness, attention, and AI trust together explain 27.5% of variance in flow suggests that these constructs are meaningful predictors but that additional factors, such as task difficulty, individual differences in flow proneness, and the specific characteristics of the learning materials, also contribute substantially to flow experience. Future research might profitably examine these additional moderating variables within an extended model. This study demonstrates that perceived usefulness of AI-generated music positively influences university students' learning engagement and flow experience through two parallel mediating pathways: attentional regulation and AI trust. Students who evaluated the AI music favourably were more likely to maintain sustained mindful awareness during academic tasks and to place greater confidence in the AI system, and both of these psychological states in turn facilitated greater engagement and immersion in learning. These findings extend TAM into the domain of AI-generated music in education and offer theoretical and practical insights into the design of AI-enhanced study environments. Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the self-reported nature of all measures introduces the possibility of common method bias. Future studies employing longitudinal designs or objective measures of attentional performance would strengthen the causal interpretation of these findings.
