analysis.discussion: This research investigated the efficacy of AI-assisted language learning instruction in enhancing English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning among Chinese EFL learners. Drawing on Vygotsky’s (1984) social constructivist theory of learning, a mixed-methods approach was employed for comprehensive data collection and analysis. The quantitative findings demonstrated a significant positive impact of AI-powered language learning instruction on the EFL learners’ English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning. Specifically, the AI-powered instruction was found to effectively improve all aspects of language learning achievement, including grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing skills. These quantitative results align with previous research conducted by Xu et al. (2022) and Zheng et al. (2021) , who also reported positive outcomes of AI-powered language learning instruction on EFL learners’ learning achievement. Additionally, the current study’s findings are consistent with the research conducted by Hsu et al. (2023) and Utami et al. (2023) , which highlighted the significant impact of AI-assisted language learning on language learners’ vocabulary knowledge and writing performance, respectively. In accordance with Vygotsky’s (1984) social constructivist theory of learning, the AI learners were initially immersed in collaborative language learning activities facilitated by the AI-assisted language learning tool, with the primary goal of enhancing their language learning achievement in grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing skills. These collaborative activities, which encompassed elements of other-regulation, played a pivotal role in assisting learners in regulating their cognitive abilities related to language achievement, leading to the gradual internalization of their learning capabilities ( Swain et al., 2015 ; Kim et al., 2018 ). In other words, the AI tool served as a catalyst, engaging learners in collaborative language learning activities that ultimately fostered the internalization of these skills ( Zheng et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2022 ). While learners in the non-AI class also internalized their language learning abilities through interactions with peers in collaborative activities, the AI learners demonstrated superior performance due to their utilization of the AI-assisted language learning tool. The AI system expedited the transition from other-regulation to self-regulation of language learning abilities, enabling AI learners to reach their ZPD or potential level of functioning earlier than anticipated ( Davis and Miyake, 2018 ). These findings align with the qualitative insights from the study, as learners corroborated the positive impact of the AI-assisted language learning tool on their independent functioning in language learning activities ( Liang et al., 2021 ). The collaborative aspect of these activities, intertwined with the AI tool’s support, played a crucial role in this transition. Moreover, the student-centered nature of language learning activities adopted in both classes likely contributed to the observed outcomes. Both groups engaged in group-work activities, while the teacher assumed the role of facilitator, encouraging students to partake in collaborative language learning endeavors. These student-centered activities positively influenced the language achievement of EFL learners in both groups ( Levine, 2004 ). However, the integration of the AI-assisted language learning tool in the AI learners’ collaborative activities appeared to be more effective in enhancing their learning achievement, synergizing the benefits of collaborative activities with the adaptive supports provided by the AI tool. This can be attributed to the AI tool’s ability to provide personalized feedback and comments on learners’ language skills, which significantly impacted their language achievement ( Kim et al., 2019 ; Liang et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2022 ). The AI system offered more effective and efficient language learning feedback, comments, and alternatives compared to other language learners, thus making a substantial contribution to learners’ language achievement ( Dodigovic, 2007 ; Kim et al., 2019 ). Although collaborative activities played a crucial role in language learning, it was the combination of collaborative activities and the adaptive supports provided by the AI tool that seemed to have the most significant impact on learners’ language achievement. The AI learners also benefited from receiving more immediate and specific feedback tailored to their own written texts. These findings further align with the qualitative insights, where learners emphasized that the AI tool provided relevant feedback and facilitated their language skill improvement at their individual pace. The high level of L2 motivation observed in AI learners may be attributed to their active engagement in interactive language learning activities facilitated by the AI system, enabling them to improve their skills at their own pace ( Hwang et al., 2020 ; Liang et al., 2021 ). This finding aligns with previous research by Utami et al. (2023) , who also reported strong motivation among language learners using AI-powered language learning activities. The qualitative findings of our study further corroborate this aspect, as participants emphasized the motivating language learning activities provided by the AI tool. The user-friendly environment created by the AI tool not only reduced language learning anxiety but also enhanced learners’ L2 motivation ( Spiro et al., 2017 ; Hsu et al., 2023 ). By offering a personalized language learning environment free from time and space restrictions, the AI tool fostered a sense of autonomy and enthusiasm in learners, thereby contributing to heightened motivation ( Carpio Cañada et al., 2015 ). In addition, one other significant outcome of this study is the evidence supporting the enhancement of self-regulated learning among Chinese EFL learners through the utilization of AI-assisted language learning instruction. Self-regulated learning, characterized by learners’ ability to independently plan, monitor, and evaluate their learning process, plays a pivotal role in fostering autonomy and lifelong learning skills ( Zimmerman, 2000 ). The integration of AI-mediated instruction has proven to be instrumental in transforming the SRL landscape, offering learners adaptive tools that empower them to take charge of their own learning process ( Xia et al., 2022b ; Jin et al., 2023 ; Wang and Lin, 2023 ). The qualitative and quantitative findings of this study converge to illuminate the positive impact of AI-assisted instruction on learners’ self-regulatory abilities. abstract_text: Although artificial intelligence (AI) has been part of our lives for some time, the launch of the Generative Pretrained Transformer (ChatGPT) has given it renewed attention. While most of these debates are about higher education in general, this article focuses on schoolteacher education and teacher training. This research aimed to determine the contribution of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in lesson planning, critical thinking and openness in education. The research used a qualitative approach and document analysis following an interpretative paradigm. The findings reveal that generative language models such as ChatGPT can provide specific materials and support mechanisms, such as lesson plans, to schoolteachers and student teachers. It also showed that ChatGPT has levelled the playing field by opening access to lesson plans to all teachers. However, to unleash their full potential for education, it is crucial to approach these models with caution and critically evaluate their limitations and potential biases, understanding that they are tools to support teaching and learning and do not replace teachers. The study’s contribution lies in ChatGPT-generated lesson plans’ implications and the enhancement of critical thinking for teacher education, and it also underscores the need for further research to explore best practices for integrating ChatGPT in lesson planning.

The findings indicate that generative language models such as ChatGPT can provide materials and support mechanisms, such as lesson plans, to teachers and student teachers. In the past, these might have been available to those in privileged contexts or who could afford to pay for such materials, services and training. ChatGPT has levelled the playing field by opening access to all teachers. The potential of ChatGPT is indeed exciting, providing new opportunities for creativity, efficiency and innovation for all. However, to unleash their full potential for education, it is crucial to approach these models with caution and critically evaluate their limitations and potential biases, understanding that they are tools to support teaching and learning. Lesson plans and related materials should be cautiously used and critiqued and adapted where needed. If ChatGPT is used by student teachers and teachers to evaluate and critique existing lessons, they might be equipped with the skills they need to succeed in the technology-driven world by focusing on applying knowledge; creating new meanings from existing knowledge; and developing skills relevant to the 21st century, such as critical thinking and problem solving. Learners need to be prepared for the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions through a comprehensive education strategy incorporating effective pedagogical strategies if education is to practice freedom. ChatGPT can be used to develop critical thinking in the form of data generation, and student teachers need to look for references to validate information and compile core arguments. The use of large language models in education is a promising area of research that offers many opportunities to support the work of teachers. The article is meant to explore how such language models, particularly ChatGPT, can assist with lesson planning and contribute to openness in teacher education. As exploratory research, it has its limitations. For example, only one lesson was used in one subject on a specific level, with no further specifications. This could have resulted in a more focused lesson plan. However, this preliminary research of AI and the latest generation of chatbot technology is believed to lead to more studies on lesson planning in different subjects and at various levels to better understand AI systems in this constantly evolving field. While this exploratory research reflects our optimism about the opportunities of large language models such as ChatGPT to transform education, it also underscores the need for further research and explore the best practices for integrating ChatGPT into lesson planning.
analysis.limitations: Despite the strides of language models such as ChatGPT, they still have limitations. For example, these models are only as good as the data they have been trained on. Therefore, it is important to acknowledge that AI systems have the potential to provide inaccurate or biased responses, be misused or inadequately deployed, and compromise data integrity and ethical standards. This means that humans are needed for continuous checking, oversight and quality assurance [2] . Authors such as Kasneci et al. [2] have further mentioned copyright issues as a challenge, indicating that, when prompting these models, they might come up with full sentences or even paragraphs of texts that they have been trained on. This can lead to copyright and plagiarism issues. Teachers and students can also misuse content from models such as ChatGPT by plagiarizing and ghostwriting [11] . For this reason, students and teachers need to have conversations about what academic integrity is and what is considered plagiarism when using AI writing tools [11] . Such conversations will contribute to their ethical and legal use, specifically in education. Another limitation is that inputs to the ChatGPT console are limited and the frequency and number of messages are throttled [7] . Additionally, it is important to realize that ChatGPT is a tool, and as Atlas [7] and Hong [8] argue, it is therefore unable to understand human emotions, intentions and reasoning. Furthermore, ChatGPT may lack a deep understanding of common-sense reasoning, which can lead to answers that sound plausible but are fundamentally incorrect or nonsensical. ChatGPT may provide answers that are factually incorrect or unverified, as it does not have real-time access to up-to-date information or the ability to browse the Internet for verification [12] . The above discussion only covered a few issues and is by no means exhaustive. We also acknowledge that, although much work still needs to be performed in terms of its limitations and challenges, large language models will continue to improve and push the boundaries of what is possible in the field of AI.

abstract_text: ChatGPT is revolutionizing the field of higher education by leveraging deep learning models to generate human-like content. However, its integration into academic settings raises concerns regarding academic integrity, plagiarism detection, and the potential impact on critical thinking skills. This article presents a study that adopts a thing ethnography approach to understand ChatGPT’s perspective on the challenges and opportunities it represents for higher education. The research explores the potential benefits and limitations of ChatGPT, as well as mitigation strategies for addressing the identified challenges. Findings emphasize the urgent need for clear policies, guidelines, and frameworks to responsibly integrate ChatGPT in higher education. It also highlights the need for empirical research to understand user experiences and perceptions. The findings provide insights that can guide future research efforts in understanding the implications of ChatGPT and similar Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems in higher education. The study concludes by highlighting the importance of thing ethnography as an innovative approach for engaging with intelligent AI systems and calls for further research to explore best practices and strategies in utilizing Generative AI for educational purposes.

analysis.methods: Ethnography refers to a form of social research that emphasizes the importance of studying first-hand what people do and say in particular contexts [18] . It involves an in-depth understanding of the world based on social relations and everyday practices. Traditionally, the focus of ethnography has been on human perspectives via qualitative methods such as observation and interviews. However, it is argued that as humans, "we have complex and intertwined relationships with the objects around us. We shape objects; and objects shape and transform our practices and us in return" [19] (p. 235). Recognizing this continual interplay between humans and objects necessitates research methodologies that grant both parties an equal role. Recently, there has been a growing interest in moving away from a human-centered ethnographic approach to that of seeking nonhuman perspectives in a context where human perspectives are felt to be partial to fully understanding the interdependent relations between humans and nonhumans [20] . By studying things as incorporated into practices, we learn about both people and objects at the same time. This approach provides the opportunity to reflect on us by reflecting on things [21] . Relatively consolidated methods for exploring the distinct viewpoints, development paths, and possible worldviews of nonhuman entities incorporate 'thing ethnography' [22] . Thing ethnography is an approach that allows access to and interpretation of things' perspectives, enabling the acquisition of novel insights into their socio-material networks. Thing ethnography emerges at the intersection of data that things give access to and the analysis and interpretation that human researchers contribute [23] . Giaccardi et al. [19] contend that adopting a thing perspective can offer distinct revelations regarding the interplay between objects and human practices, leading to novel approaches for collectively framing and resolving problems alongside these entities. In this shift towards thing ethnography, artificial intelligence (AI) plays a significant role as its unique capacities provide unprecedented access to nonhuman perspectives of the world [20] . The unique perspectives of mundane things such as kettles, cups, and scooters can now be accessed via the use of software and sensors [21, 23] . For instance, by attaching autographers to kettles, fridges, and cups, a study collected more than 3000 photographs that helped to uncover use patterns and home practices around these objects [21] . Another study looking into the design of thoughtful forms of smart mobility used cameras and sensors to collect data from scooters in Taipei, generating a better understanding of the socio-material networks among scooters and scooterists in Taiwan [23] . Moreover, the development of chatbots opens the possibility of directly interacting and accessing AI systems' views via text exchange. It has already been recognized that AI "has the potential to impact our lives and our world as no other technology has done before" [24] , both positively and negatively. This knowledge is raising many questions concerning its ethical, legal, and socio-economic effects, and even calls for a pause in the development of more advanced AI systems [25] . With the increasing intelligence of things, it becomes crucial to adopt suitable perspectives to access, observe and understand the diverse social consequences and emerging possibilities that arise from this advancement [23] . So far, the relationship between humans and things in research has been unidirectional [19] . So, what happens if we change the focus to 'things', especially 'things' with human-like intelligence with the potential to become fully self-aware within the next few decades or even achieve Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) [26, 27] ? What happens if we try to understand the world from the perspective of a 'thing', such as AI, which is increasingly impacting many aspects of life? Applying thing ethnography to the study of AI systems can aid in exploring their social and cultural dimensions and their impact on society from their own perspective. In this context, we argue that ChatGPT should not be studied merely as an "object" designed, trained, and used by people but as a "subject" that co-performs daily practices with users and has an impact on the socio-material networks in which it is embedded. In the case of thing ethnography applied to ChatGPT, the focus would be on understanding the user experience, the impact on communication dynamics, and the broader societal implications from ChatGPT's perspective. A better understanding of this can help guide the development and deployment of chatbot technologies in a way that is more responsive to user needs, respects societal values, and promotes responsible AI practices. We believe that thing ethnography approaches are becoming crucially relevant as efforts attempting to build successively more powerful AI systems closer to AGI-AI systems that are generally smarter than humans-continue [27] . As 'things' become increasingly intelligent, there is an unprecedented and pressing demand to enhance our ability to access and comprehend the perspective of these entities. In this study, we apply thing ethnography to engage with ChatGPT. Whereas previous thing ethnography interventions have used different smart devices to access the perspective of things, our study will engage with the 'subject' via a written conversation given the unique text generation capacities of chatbots. To answer the research questions stated in the previous section, this study has adopted a semi-structured interview. This type of interview facilitates the collection of rich data related to participants' views [28] , with the required degree of structure and flexibility [29] . An interview guide containing a list of themes and key questions was prepared before the interview. Nevertheless, the flexibility of semi-structured interviewing allowed the use of probes devised during the interviews. Probing is useful to further explore responses that are deemed significant for the research topic [28] . In line with King and Horrocks' [30] suggestion, probing was adopted to seek clarification for unclear words or phrases, completion for stories that the interviewer felt unfinished, and elaboration to encourage the interviewee to 'keep talking'. The six-phase thematic analysis approach proposed by Braun and Clarke [31] formed the foundation for analyzing data from the semi-structured interview. This approach provided guidance for coding and categorizing the data, enabling a systematic, thorough, and cumulative analysis of the case study information. During the reporting phase, we aimed for dependability and transparency by providing verbatim quotes linked to specific codes being analyzed. These links are what connect raw data to "the data summary and interpretation generated by the researcher" [32] (p. 95). Additionally, we addressed transferability by comparing the emerging findings with the existing body of literature [33] . This was accomplished by examining similarities, contradictions, and their underlying reasons. This approach can lead to broader applicability and increased credibility of qualitative data.

The findings of this study highlighted the transformative potential of ChatGPT in education, consistent with previous studies, while also revealing additional insights. It also highlighted significant challenges that must be addressed. The paper presents key themes identified during the interview, including opportunities, challenges, barriers, and mitigation strategies. Given the novelty of ChatGPT, existing literature about its use within higher education is limited and largely hypothetical or speculative. Our hope is that the findings presented here can serve as a research agenda for researchers and the wider academic community to identify research priorities, gaps in knowledge, and emerging trends. A key takeaway point is the urgent need for empirical research that delves into best practices and strategies for maximizing the benefits of GenAI, as well as user experiences, to understand students' and academics' perceptions, concerns, and interactions with ChatGPT. Another priority is the development of policies, guidelines, and frameworks for the responsible integration of ChatGPT in higher education. Based on the conversation with ChatGPT, this paper also presents some principles for the acceptable and responsible use of AI in higher education. These principles can be useful for Higher Education Institutions working towards internal AI policies. However, empirical studies are needed to explore the transferability of findings presented here to varied contexts with specific features, for instance, distance or online learning. This study employed a thing ethnography approach to explore ChatGPT's perspective on the opportunities and challenges it presents for higher education. This is an innovative approach that has been implemented in design research but could become a powerful tool for researchers from other disciplines wanting to engage with "intelligent things". In this study, thing ethnography provided a methodological framework to collect the viewpoints of ChatGPT. This helped us to test its potential biases and accuracy, as well as uncover insights that have not been extensively documented in the existing literature. As an interviewee, ChatGPT provided very relevant and interesting insights, showing some level of critique towards itself when questioned about potential risks and challenges, which indicates some level of transparency regarding its own shortcomings. A benefit of this approach is that ChatGPT enables interviewers to request further information and clarify responses, which can enhance data collection. Additionally, the chatbot displays a very good level of recollection during a conversation. Its memory seems to be limited; however, this did not represent an issue for the length of our interview. Despite the absence of non-verbal cues and expressions, the answers obtained seemed balanced and clearly conveyed meaning. Therefore, it is argued that interviews with ChatGPT have the potential to collect relevant data. Limitations inherent to ethnographic research [50] are also applicable to thing ethnography and, therefore, to this study. The first one relates to the limited scope and selection bias; ethnographic research usually focuses on specific individuals, groups, or communities. In this study, there is a strong focus on ChatGPT as a form of GenAI. However, other GenAI chatbots, such as Bard or Bing Chat, have recently emerged and become accessible to the public. Thus, the findings presented here may not be representative of the views of all existing GenAI chatbots. Future interactions could aim to compare the views from different GenAI chats to find similarities and discrepancies. This could provide us with a more holistic understanding of GenAI chatbots' perspectives in the context of higher education. Another limitation could be the replicability of results; even though the interview can be easily replicated, it is still not clear that ChatGPT will provide the same answers. As consecutive and improved versions of ChatGPT are released, there will be a need to replicate interventions such as the one proposed here to test for stability in the findings. Another limitation relates to the potential research bias during the analysis of data. The audit trail was particularly important in increasing the dependability and transparency of thematic analysis [32] . A significant aspect of documenting this process is providing verbatim quotes linked to specific codes. These links are what connect participants' words (i.e., raw data) to "the data summary and interpretation generated by the researcher" [32] (p. 95). This approach can increase the capacity of external reviewers to judge the research findings fairly. Furthermore, transferability was addressed by comparing emerging results with existing literature [33] . Lastly, ethnographic studies tend to be highly immersive and lengthy, requiring extended periods in the field to gain an in-depth understanding of the research subject. However, thing ethnography does not necessarily require a longitudinal research design and cross-sectional research designs, where data is collected at one point in time, have been documented [21, 23] . In this context, we see the intervention reported here as the first step in a broader research study. The next steps include further conversations with ChatGPT, and other chatbots, to test the replicability of findings presented here and the exploration of more topics not covered in the initial interview. We believe the use of thing ethnography to engage with ChatGPT is very relevant and would encourage other researchers to involve GenAI entities in the process of collectively framing and resolving current challenges. Our argument is that ChatGPT should be approached not merely as an object controlled by humans but as a subject actively engaging in daily practices alongside users, influencing communication dynamics, and impacting socio-material networks.

Second, the relevant evidence is methodologically heterogeneous (EEG experiments, randomised trials, surveys, phenomenological studies, tool evaluations, and conceptual analyses), which precludes meta-analysis. Third, the GenAI literature is very recent and fast-moving, so the review prioritises critical interpretation of a verified, purposively assembled corpus over exhaustive coverage. Thematic synthesis was chosen because it moves transparently from descriptive coding of individual sources to analytic themes that address the review's own research questions (Thomas and Harden, 2008) . An earlier draft of this manuscript was found, on review, to contain a reference list built substantially from fabricated citationsinvented titles and journals attached to real author surnames, in several cases combining names from unrelated papers into fictitious composite references. That draft's bibliography has been discarded in its entirety and rebuilt from independently verified sources. Several features of the evidence base may explain variation in findings. Measurement differs: self-reported effort (Gerlich, 2025; Lee et al., 2025) and neural connectivity (Kosmyna et al., 2025) are not measures of critical thinking, and only a few studies measure delayed or transfer outcomes. Populations differ: knowledge workers, university students, and secondary-school students bring different prior knowledge, which theory suggests should change how much they can scrutinise AI output. Tool design differs: unguided chatbots and guardrailed tutors are not the same intervention (Bastani et al., 2025) . Context differs: samples come from the United States, Europe, Australia, China, Turkey, and Bangladesh, with different assessment cultures and AI policies, but few studies compare contexts directly. Finally, most studies capture single sessions or a single term, whereas the concern about critical thinking is cumulative.
analysis.discussion: This review set out to examine how information abundance, algorithmic curation, and GenAI use may influence critical thinking in higher education, and what universities should therefore teach and assess. Across five themes, the synthesis suggests that the central cognitive task for students has shifted from retrieving information to evaluating it; that unguided GenAI use is associated with reduced cognitive engagement and, in several experiments, with performance gains that do not translate into independent learning; that fluent AI output is readily mistaken for validated knowledge, while automated detection is too unreliable and biased to serve as a remedy; that critical thinking and lateral reading are teachable and that guided AI use and process-visible assessment are promising responses; and that workload, equity, and policy constraints shape which institutions can adopt them. The evidence establishes some of these claims more firmly than others. It establishes that language models hallucinate, that AI detectors are unreliable and biased, and that critical thinking and lateral reading can be taught. It suggests, with growing but still short-term support, that unguided AI use reduces cognitive effort and can dissociate performance from learning, and that tool design moderates this. It remains uncertain whether these effects accumulate into lasting declines in critical thinking, how critical thinking should be measured when AI is part of the task, and whether process-visible assessment improves outcomes in practice. Theoretically, the synthesis refines several perspectives at once. It distinguishes offloading that reduces extraneous load from offloading that removes the germane processing through which learning occurs; it proposes fading as a design criterion for AI tools, extending scaffolding theory; it specifies four dimensions of critical thinking matched to the mechanisms they counteract; it extends information literacy from evaluating sources to auditing AI output; and it identifies calibrated trust in AI as a target for self-regulated learning. analysis.limitations: This review synthesizes 45 purposively identified sources rather than a systematically searched, exhaustive literature base, and it should not be read as a comprehensive systematic review of a fast-moving field. No structured search of Scopus or Web of Science with PRISMA-style screening was conducted, so the search cannot be fully reproduced, and relevant studies may have been missed. Coding was conducted by a single reviewer, so inter-coder agreement could not be assessed, although the source-by-theme matrix and evidence-strength judgements are reported to make the interpretation auditable. No formal riskof-bias instrument was applied. Several of the most directly relevant empirical sources (Kosmyna et al., 2025; Roy and Jony, 2026) are very recent, and at least one (Kosmyna et al., 2025) has drawn published methodological criticism regarding sample size and analytic transparency that this review has not independently adjudicated; its findings are reported here as suggestive rather than settled. The strongest experimental evidence on delayed effects comes from a secondary-school sample (Bastani et al., 2025) . The proposed connections between classical cognitive science and contemporary GenAI-specific findings are this review's own interpretive synthesis rather than a claim directly tested by any single included study. Finally, only English-language sources were included, and although the corpus includes studies from Asia and the Middle East as well as Western contexts, most sources come from Western highereducation systems, limiting confidence in how far the findings generalize elsewhere. A further limitation concerns the scaffolding-fade component of the framework: while the underlying scaffolding literature (Vygotsky, 1978; Wood, Bruner, and Ross, 1976) is well established, its application to generative AI specifically is this review's own extension, and empirical work directly testing whether AI tools can be redesigned to fade in the way human scaffolding does remains largely absent from the current literature. The Fade-Visibility Matrix is likewise unvalidated; Section 6.4 sets out propositions for testing it, and a systematic review with a registered protocol is a natural next step.

abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support academic performance while also creating a perceived gap between AI-supported task completion and independently available competence. This study examined how multidimensional critical thinking dispositions are associated with cognitive offloading, cognitive enhancement, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy (PSD) in GenAI-assisted learning. analysis.discussion: This study estimated differentiated associations between five critical thinking dispositions, two GenAI interaction pathways, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy. The findings are consistent with several propositions derived from distributed cognition and depth-of-processing perspectives, while the cross-sectional and self-report design limits causal and mechanistic interpretation. This study examined the associations among five dimensions of critical thinking disposition, cognitive offloading, cognitive enhancement, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy in GenAI-assisted academic learning. Inquisitiveness was positively associated with both interaction pathways, whereas open-mindedness and systematicity showed small positive associations with cognitive enhancement. Analyticity and truth-seeking were not significantly associated with either cognitive offloading or cognitive enhancement. Both interaction pathways were positively associated with perceived supportdependence discrepancy, although the association was stronger for cognitive offloading. The findings contribute to research on learner-AI interaction by distinguishing cognitively substitutive and cognitively constructive forms of GenAI engagement while recognizing that they may coexist. The significant indirect associations further indicate that critical thinking dispositions may be linked to perceived supported-versusunsupported competence through different patterns of human-AI interaction. However, the study assessed perceived support-dependence discrepancy as a monitoring-related self-report rather than as a direct measure of metacognitive monitoring, cognitive ownership, or objective calibration. The present findings should therefore be interpreted as associations with a perceived support-dependent competence gap rather than as evidence of any single established psychological mechanism. Academic stress did not significantly moderate the association between cognitive offloading and perceived support-dependence discrepancy in the present observed-score analysis. This result indicates only that the hypothesized moderation was not detected in the current sample and does not establish invariance across tasks, institutions, or stress conditions. Given the cross-sectional design, single-item outcome measure, common data source, and heterogeneous task contexts, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of conditional statistical associations. Longitudinal, behavioral, and experimental studies incorporating AI-assisted performance, unaided performance, confidence judgments, and validated support-dependence measures are needed to test the direction and mechanisms of these relationships.
analysis.limitations: First, academic stress and perceived support-dependence discrepancy were measured with single items. Reliability sensitivity analyses showed that the focal latent-path conclusions were stable across several assumed reliability values, but this does not substitute for direct evidence of reliability, construct coverage, or measurement validity. The PSD item captures learners' perceived awareness of a gap between AI-supported and unaided competence; it does not directly measure the accuracy of ongoing judgments about understanding or independent reproducibility, nor does it establish illusory self-assessment, overconfidence, or objectively verified calibration bias. Future studies should develop and validate separate multi-item measures of perceived support-dependence discrepancy and metacognitive monitoring and combine them with repeated confidence judgments, AIassisted performance scores, delayed unaided performance scores, and objective calibration indices. Second, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal or causal ordering. Structural paths and indirect associations should be interpreted as conditional covariance patterns under the specified model. Longitudinal panels, cross-lagged designs, randomized interventions, and delayed transfer tests are needed to evaluate directionality. Third, convergent and discriminant validity were not uniformly strong. Three AVE values were below 0.50, and several critical-thinking dimensions showed high HTMT values and semantically overlapping items. Future measurement studies should revise overlapping items, confirm the factor structure in an independent sample, assess convergent and incremental validity against established AI-literacy and GenAI-use measures, and test measurement invariance across institutions and disciplines. Fourth, all focal variables came from the same questionnaire. Procedural controls and the common-method-factor analysis reduced but did not eliminate common-method concerns. Future studies should combine self-reports with prompt logs, source-check records, think-aloud protocols, instructor ratings, and objective transfer tasks to determine whether reported interaction patterns correspond to observable behavior. Fifth, participants answered with reference to usual academic tasks rather than a standardized task, so task type, complexity, discipline, and permitted assistance may be confounded. Future research should use standardized tasks and systematically vary or record task complexity, disciplinary context, and the permitted level of GenAI assistance to test whether the observed associations are task-contingent. Sixth, although the stratified purposive sampling strategy provided variation across regions and institution types, the sample was not probability-based. Future multicenter studies should adopt probability-based or clearly enumerated sampling frames, document institutionspecific recruitment and exclusions, and test the model across a broader range of regions and institutions. The findings should therefore be generalized beyond the participating universities with caution.

analysis.discussion: This study investigated the psychological mechanisms underlying undergraduate students' overreliance on GAI feedback by integrating perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive monitoring into a unified research model. Based on survey data from university students, this study examined how learning-related cognitive demands influence students' use of GAI and how cognitive offloading contributes to the formation of GAI feedback dependence. The findings provide a cognitive perspective for understanding students' interaction with generative artificial intelligence in learning environments. The results demonstrate that perceived cognitive load plays an important role in shaping students' GAI-related behaviors. When students experience higher cognitive demands during learning, they are more likely to adopt cognitive offloading strategies by using GAI as external cognitive support. Cognitive offloading further contributes to overreliance on GAI feedback, indicating that students' dependence on AI feedback is not only related to technological factors but also reflects their cognitive responses to learning pressure. In addition, perceived cognitive load directly influences overreliance on GAI feedback, suggesting that cognitive demands can affect students' reliance on AI-generated information through both direct and indirect pathways. Furthermore, this study reveals the role of metacognitive monitoring in shaping the relationship between cognitive demands and GAI feedback dependence. The comparison between groups with different levels of metacognitive monitoring shows that students follow different pathways when developing reliance on GAI feedback. Students with lower metacognitive monitoring show a stronger direct association between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance, whereas students with higher metacognitive monitoring show a stronger role of cognitive offloading in explaining GAI feedback dependence. These findings suggest that metacognitive monitoring influences not only students' learning regulation but also how they manage their cognitive relationship with intelligent tools. Overall, this study extends the understanding of GAIsupported learning by demonstrating that overreliance on AI feedback emerges from the interaction between cognitive demands, external cognitive support, and self-regulatory processes. The findings highlight that effective GAI use requires more than access to intelligent tools; it also depends on students' ability to regulate cognitive resources and evaluate AI-generated information appropriately. This study provides theoretical and practical insights into how university students can develop a more balanced and productive relationship with generative artificial intelligence in learning contexts.
analysis.limitations: Although this study reveals the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, metacognitive monitoring, and overreliance on GAI feedback, several aspects require further investigation. First, the cross-sectional design of this study limits the ability to establish causal relationships among the variables. Although the structural equation model supports the hypothesized associations and mediation pathways, the findings should be interpreted as relationships among variables rather than causal effects. Students' interactions with GAI may involve dynamic processes in which cognitive load, cognitive offloading strategies, metacognitive monitoring, and feedback reliance influence each other over time. Future studies could adopt longitudinal designs, experimental methods, or experience sampling approaches to further examine the developmental and causal mechanisms underlying students' interactions with GAI. Second, this study used a single-item measure to classify students' metacognitive monitoring levels. Although this approach provides a concise indicator of students' perceived metacognitive monitoring and facilitates comparisons between groups, it may not fully capture the complexity and multidimensional characteristics of metacognitive monitoring. Metacognitive monitoring involves various processes, including monitoring understanding, evaluating learning progress, and regulating cognitive strategies, which may not be sufficiently represented by a single item. Future research could employ validated multi-item scales or combine selfreported measures with behavioral indicators to obtain a more comprehensive assessment of students' metacognitive monitoring abilities. Third, the comparisons between the low-and high-metacognitive-monitoring groups in this study were based on differences in path coefficient patterns rather than formal statistical tests of betweengroup differences. Therefore, these results should be interpreted as variations in structural relationships across metacognitive monitoring levels rather than confirmed differences between groups. Future research could apply formal multi-group analysis approaches to further examine whether the strength of relationships among variables significantly differs across different levels of metacognitive monitoring. Fourth, the present study mainly relied on self-reported questionnaires to measure students' GAI use experiences, cognitive perceptions, and behavioral tendencies. Although self-reported measures are useful for capturing students' subjective experiences, they may also be influenced by recall bias, social desirability, and individual interpretation differences, which may introduce potential common method bias. Future research could integrate multiple data sources, such as GAI interaction logs, learning behavior records, task performance data, and experimental measures, to provide a more objective understanding of students' cognitive regulation processes during GAI use. Finally, the participants in this study were recruited from a single university, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Students from different universities, academic disciplines, and educational contexts may differ in their access to AI technologies, learning environments, and patterns of GAI engagement. Therefore, future studies should include samples from multiple institutions and diverse educational backgrounds to further validate the proposed model and examine its applicability across different learning contexts.

In terms of academic year, 183 were first-year students (27.5%), 159 were second-year students (23.9%), 172 were third-year students (25.9%), and 151 were fourth-year students (22.7%). The resulting participant-to-item ratio was approximately 25.6:1, providing a substantial empirical basis for estimating the factor structure. For Study 1, the questionnaire was distributed online through student groups and class groups associated with several universities using a convenience sampling approach. Before participation, students were informed of the study purpose, the voluntary nature of participation, confidentiality of responses, and the scientific use of the data. The AI Cognitive Offloading Scale for College Students (AI-COS) was developed through sequential stages. First, the construct definition and provisional dimensional structure were established through literature review and theoretical analysis of cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, transactive memory, and AI-assisted learning. No formal open-ended or semi-structured interviews were conducted, and no separate pilot study was conducted before the main survey. Second, an initial pool of 26 items was generated and refined for clarity, conciseness, conceptual relevance, and appropriateness to college learning contexts. Third, a panel of five experts (all holding Ph.D. degrees in Psychology or Educational Technology, with average professional academic experience exceeding 5 years) independently evaluated all 26 items using a 3-point relevance scale (1 = inappropriate, 2 = appropriate after revision, 3 = appropriate). Their judgments focused on conceptual relevance, representativeness of AI cognitive offloading, wording clarity, and suitability for college learning contexts. The item wording and conceptual fit were revised in response to this evaluation, and the 26-item preliminary questionnaire was retained for empirical evaluation. Fourth, the preliminary questionnaire was evaluated empirically in the Study 1 sample through item discrimination, item-total correlations, and reliability analysis before EFA. Thus, preliminary questionnaire evaluation in the present study refers to expert content evaluation followed by empirical item analysis rather than to a separate pilot sample. A 5point Likert response format ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree" was used. Finally, SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.3 were used for item analysis and EFA. Participants for Study 2 were recruited from several universities through university student groups and class groups using the same convenience sampling approach as in Study 1. The questionnaire was administered online. Referring to the commonly used method (Curran, 2016; Xu and Li, 2021) , 58 participants whose answers were incomplete were excluded, leaving 1,123 valid participants. The final sample consisted of 1,123 valid participants, including 563 males (50.1%) and 560 females (49.9%). Regarding academic standing, 288 participants were first-year students (25.6%), 290 were second-year students (25.8%), 269 were third-year students (24.0%), and 276 were fourth-year students (24.6%). For Study 2, the questionnaire was distributed online through student groups and class groups associated with several universities, using the same convenience-sampling procedure as in Study 1. The Study 2 participants were newly recruited and did not overlap with the Study 1 sample. Before completing the questionnaire, participants were informed that participation was voluntary, responses would remain confidential, and the data would be used only for scientific research. analysis.discussion: The present study developed and validated the AI Cognitive Offloading Scale for College Students (AI-COS) by examining how different cognitive functions are delegated to generative AI in learning contexts. The contribution should be understood as an alternative and context-specific operationalization rather than as the first measurement of AI cognitive offloading. Recent work has already provided complementary approaches. Jiang and Chen (2026) developed the AIBCO Scale for highereducation students in China, distinguishing lower-order from higher-order cognitive offloading according to the level of cognitive demand. Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent from autonomous cognitive offloading according to whether users substitute their own thinking or use AI as a scaffold while retaining cognitive agency. In contrast, the AI-COS organizes offloading by the primary cognitive function delegated to AI-memory, assistive task-related processing, and thinking-and was developed specifically for Chinese college students' learning activities. These distinctions make the AI-COS conceptually complementary to existing measures: the AIBCO framework emphasizes cognitivedemand level, the dependent/autonomous framework emphasizes the manner of delegation, and the AI-COS emphasizes the function being delegated. This function-based perspective may be useful when researchers need to distinguish information storage and retrieval from AI participation in academic task execution and from delegation of judgment or decision support. From a theoretical standpoint, the findings suggest that the influence of generative AI on college students' learning is no longer confined to information provision or efficiency enhancement. Rather, AI systems can be implicated in task execution, cognitive processing, and intellectual regulation, functioning as components of an extended cognitive system. The extended mind theory argues that external tools are not merely ancillary to cognition, but may become constitutive elements of the cognitive system itself (Clark and Chalmers, 1998) . Likewise, cognitive offloading research indicates that external resources can reduce internal cognitive load, while the consequences of offloading may depend on the nature and regulation of the delegated activity (Risko and Gilbert, 2016; Turner, 2022) . Within this framework, the present study conceptualized three functionally distinct forms of AI cognitive offloading-memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading. These dimensions describe different cognitive functions that may be delegated to AI; the present cross-sectional factor structure does not establish that students move from one form to another over time. One of the important findings is that AI cognitive offloading among college students can be differentiated into three interrelated dimensions: memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading. Importantly, this three-dimensional structure represents one empirically supported operationalization of the construct rather than a claim that these are the only possible dimensions. The exploratory factor analysis yielded a clear factor pattern, and the confirmatory factor analysis supported a higherorder structure. The resulting dimensions are also conceptually distinguishable from recent alternatives. Jiang and Chen (2026) separated AI-based cognitive offloading into lower-order and higher-order forms, while Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent and autonomous offloading according to the degree to which users retain cognitive agency. The AI-COS instead differentiates the functions delegated to AI within college learning: memory-related storage and retrieval, task-related assistance and execution, and higher-order thinking-related judgment and decision support. The three approaches therefore address related but non-identical questions about AI-mediated cognition. TABLE Fit indices and testing for measurement invariance across groups. Within this framework, memory offloading primarily reflects students' tendency to delegate basic cognitive operations-such as memorization, retrieval, storage, and organization-to AI systems, thereby transferring part of the cognitive burden to external technological resources. This dimension is closely aligned with the classic notion of cognitive offloading, namely the use of external media to reduce internal cognitive costs. Assistive offloading, in contrast, involves AI-supported completion and organization of learning tasks, including content generation, textual organization, expression refinement, and the handling of complex academic assignments. Thinking offloading involves the delegation of judgment support, analytic integration, logical inference, and decision assistance. These dimensions therefore differ in the type of cognitive function being delegated, but the present factor analysis does not demonstrate that they form a developmental continuum, that one dimension necessarily precedes another, or that greater endorsement of one dimension causes movement toward another. Their co-occurrence under a higher-order factor indicates shared variance in AI cognitive offloading, not temporal progression. The confirmatory factor analysis further supported the proposed multidimensional structure. The second-order model provided the best fit among the three competing specifications, and the three first-order dimensions showed strong loadings on the higher-order AI cognitive offloading factor. This pattern supports a hierarchical representation in which memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading are distinguishable functions that share substantial common variance. The model therefore provides a statistical basis for reporting both dimension-specific scores and an overall AI cognitive offloading score. Importantly, the higher-order representation should not be interpreted as evidence that the three dimensions form a temporal sequence or a developmental hierarchy. The criterion-related validity findings are particularly informative because they reveal differentiated association patterns across dimensions. The total AI cognitive offloading score and all three dimensions showed significant positive associations with AI dependence, indicating that greater reported AI cognitive offloading was associated with greater AI dependence across the three function-based forms. Similarly, the total score and all three dimensions were negatively associated with metacognitive monitoring. In relation to need for cognition, the total score and assistive offloading were negatively associated with need for cognition, whereas the memory and thinking offloading dimensions were not significantly related to this criterion. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence that cognitive offloading is inherently beneficial or detrimental. Instead, they suggest that the psychological meaning of offloading may depend on which cognitive function is delegated, the extent of delegation, and the degree to which learners continue to monitor and regulate the process. From a functional perspective, cognitive offloading may enhance cognition when external resources reduce unnecessary cognitive demands, support information organization and retrieval, or free internal resources for monitoring, integration, and other higher-order activities (Risko and Gilbert, 2016; Dunn and Risko, 2016) . analysis.limitations: Although the present study provides relatively comprehensive evidence for the development and validation of the scale, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although the sample included a relatively large number of college students, it was still drawn primarily from undergraduate students in a specific contextual setting. Future studies should therefore further examine the external validity of the scale across different regions, types of institutions, and graduate student populations. Second, the present study employed a cross-sectional design, which does not allow for the examination of dynamic changes in AI cognitive offloading during the learning process, nor does it permit causal inference regarding its antecedents or consequences. Third, although the current scale distinguishes among memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading, the rapid evolution of generative AI may continue to reshape how students use such systems. Future research should therefore revise and refine the items in light of new model capabilities, task contexts, and educational norms. Fourth, the initial item-development stage was based on literature review, theoretical analysis, and expert content evaluation rather than formal qualitative interviews. Therefore, the present study does not provide interview-derived qualitative evidence for item generation. Future scale-development studies could incorporate systematic open-ended interviews or focus groups, together with detailed coding procedures, to further examine students' lived experiences of AI cognitive offloading and whether additional dimensions or context-specific behaviors should be represented. Combining qualitative exploration with quantitative validation has been illustrated in other domains, such as the development of a multidimensional career-success scale for Chinese employees (Zhou et al., 2013) , and offers a methodological example for future scale refinement. Fifth, future research may also combine interviews, learning logs, or behavioral data to examine whether different forms of AI cognitive offloading correspond to different actual learning outcomes, thereby gradually extending this construct from a self-report measure toward a multi-method assessment framework. Future assessments could also distinguish metacognitive knowledge, monitoring, and control and incorporate taskbased measures alongside self-report, drawing on measurement approaches reviewed in educational settings (Rivers et al., 2020) . Sixth, although three dimensions were retained, their coverage of AI cognitive offloading should be examined further across tasks, populations, and contexts. Unexplained item variance may reflect specific variance and measurement error as well as other influences. Existing research suggests that AI cognitive offloading may also vary according to the cognitive-demand level of the delegated task and the manner in which users engage with AI. For example, Jiang and Chen (2026) distinguished lower-order and higher-order AI cognitive offloading and showed that AI evaluation capability may condition associations with these forms, whereas Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent from autonomous offloading according to whether users retain cognitive agency. Future research should therefore examine whether cognitive-demand level, delegation style, AI evaluation capability, task characteristics, and learner characteristics account for additional variance or function as antecedents and boundary conditions of AI cognitive offloading. Longitudinal, experimental, behavioral, and cross-context validation studies may help determine whether these dimensions represent additional components of the construct or complementary dimensions that operate alongside the function-based structure identified in the present study. Existing reviews also suggest that this field remains in a phase of rapid expansion but uneven evidence development, underscoring the need for structured measurement tools such as the present scale to address the current gap at the level of cognitive processes (Schei et al., 2024; McDonald et al., 2025) . A review of early public claims about ChatGPT highlights the need to distinguish expectations about educational transformation from empirical evidence (Jensen et al., 2025) . A review of empirical studies further identified heterogeneous approaches and limited shared theoretical grounding in research on generative AI chatbots in higher education (McGrath et al., 2025) .

reading.findings: The central insight emerging from this research is that generative AI does not merely change how quickly or easily knowledge work is performed; it can also change the relation between creators and their own cognitive processes. When AI systems produce fluent, complete, and seemingly reasonable outputs, individuals reduce not only routine Moderating effect of task complexity on the relationship between metacognitive disengagement and knowledge innovation quality: simple slope analyses. cognitive operations but also the planning, monitoring, and reflection that would otherwise accompany their own intellectual work. Importantly, metacognitive disengagement does not imply the absence of thought. Rather, it describes a systematic decline in the depth of metacognitive investment: individuals may still read, select, and even revise AI outputs, but they are less likely to question underlying assumptions, compare alternatives, or reflect on their own strategies. This partial engagement is precisely what makes metacognitive disengagement difficult to observe, yet sufficient to erode the deeper cognitive processing required for knowledge innovation. These findings extend the classic argument of Salomon and Perkins (1989) that intelligent technologies can invite users to transfer thinking responsibility to the tool. Generative AI makes this tendency more consequential because it can perform not only peripheral cognitive tasks but also core operations such as inference, synthesis, and evaluation. The resulting shift from offloading memory to offloading thinking represents a qualitatively new phase of cognitive offloading (Risko and Gilbert, 2016) . Our results suggest that the most important cost of this shift may not be a direct decline in task performance, but a gradual retreat from the metacognitive regulation that sustains longterm creative capability. From a metacognition perspective, the present findings extend prior work that has linked metacognitive processes to complex problem solving and creative performance (Flavell, 1979; Schraw and Moshman, 1995) . We show that in human-AI collaboration, metacognitive engagement depends not only on individual ability but also on the technological conditions under which knowledge work is performed. When AI assumes the cognitive operations that metacognitive monitoring would ordinarily track, the raw material for monitoring disappears; when AI is perceived as reliable, the perceived necessity of monitoring declines (de Visser et al., 2016) . This dual erosion mechanism provides a more specific account of how AI use can reduce cognitive engagement, going beyond existing discussions of metacognitive laziness in learning contexts (Fan et al., 2025) . Participants in the high-assistance condition showed significantly higher levels of planning reduction, monitoring weakening, and reflection absence than those in the lowassistance condition, supporting H1. A particularly interesting finding was that greater familiarity with AI was associated with lower, rather than higher, metacognitive disengagement. This pattern runs counter to the intuitive expectation that familiarity breeds dependency. One possible explanation is that individuals who are more familiar with AI are also more aware of its limitations and therefore more likely to maintain critical engagement and metacognitive vigilance when using it. This interpretation points to AI literacy as a potentially important buffer against metacognitive disengagement, which informed the inclusion of individual AI literacy as a moderator in later experiments. Experiment 2 replicated the main effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement in a different task context and provided evidence for the mediating role of cognitive offloading. Higher AI assistance increased cognitive offloading, which in turn strengthened metacognitive disengagement. Under high AI assistance, individuals outsourced core cognitive tasks such as information retrieval, framework construction, and solution generation, reducing their direct participation in the cognitive process. This offloading deprived metacognitive monitoring of its raw material and weakened the perceived necessity of self-checking, thereby producing a chain from cognitive offloading through reduced metacognitive engagement to metacognitive disengagement. analysis.results: The central insight emerging from this research is that generative AI does not merely change how quickly or easily knowledge work is performed; it can also change the relation between creators and their own cognitive processes. When AI systems produce fluent, complete, and seemingly reasonable outputs, individuals reduce not only routine Moderating effect of task complexity on the relationship between metacognitive disengagement and knowledge innovation quality: simple slope analyses. cognitive operations but also the planning, monitoring, and reflection that would otherwise accompany their own intellectual work. Importantly, metacognitive disengagement does not imply the absence of thought. Rather, it describes a systematic decline in the depth of metacognitive investment: individuals may still read, select, and even revise AI outputs, but they are less likely to question underlying assumptions, compare alternatives, or reflect on their own strategies. This partial engagement is precisely what makes metacognitive disengagement difficult to observe, yet sufficient to erode the deeper cognitive processing required for knowledge innovation. These findings extend the classic argument of Salomon and Perkins (1989) that intelligent technologies can invite users to transfer thinking responsibility to the tool. Generative AI makes this tendency more consequential because it can perform not only peripheral cognitive tasks but also core operations such as inference, synthesis, and evaluation. The resulting shift from offloading memory to offloading thinking represents a qualitatively new phase of cognitive offloading (Risko and Gilbert, 2016) . Our results suggest that the most important cost of this shift may not be a direct decline in task performance, but a gradual retreat from the metacognitive regulation that sustains longterm creative capability. From a metacognition perspective, the present findings extend prior work that has linked metacognitive processes to complex problem solving and creative performance (Flavell, 1979; Schraw and Moshman, 1995) . We show that in human-AI collaboration, metacognitive engagement depends not only on individual ability but also on the technological conditions under which knowledge work is performed. When AI assumes the cognitive operations that metacognitive monitoring would ordinarily track, the raw material for monitoring disappears; when AI is perceived as reliable, the perceived necessity of monitoring declines (de Visser et al., 2016) . This dual erosion mechanism provides a more specific account of how AI use can reduce cognitive engagement, going beyond existing discussions of metacognitive laziness in learning contexts (Fan et al., 2025) . It is also noteworthy that cognitive offloading only partially mediated the effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement and the effect of cognitive offloading on innovation quality. This partial mediation indicates that other mechanisms are likely involved. For example, when creators delegate primary cognitive responsibility to AI, their self-efficacy may shift from a sense of having solved the problem themselves to a sense of merely supervising the AI that solved it, and their sense of accountability for the output may weaken. These possibilities are consistent with the automation-augmentation paradox identified in management research (Raisch and Krakowski, 2021) , in which the same AI system can either substitute for human cognition or augment it depending on how it is integrated into work processes.
analysis.discussion: Experiment 1 provided initial evidence for the main effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement in human-AI collaborative knowledge innovation. Participants in the high-assistance condition showed significantly higher levels of planning reduction, monitoring weakening, and reflection absence than those in the lowassistance condition, supporting H1. A particularly interesting finding was that greater familiarity with AI was associated with lower, rather than higher, metacognitive disengagement. This pattern runs counter to the intuitive expectation that familiarity breeds dependency. One possible explanation is that individuals who are more familiar with AI are also more aware of its limitations and therefore more likely to maintain critical engagement and metacognitive vigilance when using it. This interpretation points to AI literacy as a potentially important buffer against metacognitive disengagement, which informed the inclusion of individual AI literacy as a moderator in later experiments. Experiment 2 replicated the main effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement in a different task context and provided evidence for the mediating role of cognitive offloading. Higher AI assistance increased cognitive offloading, which in turn strengthened metacognitive disengagement. Under high AI assistance, individuals outsourced core cognitive tasks such as information retrieval, framework construction, and solution generation, reducing their direct participation in the cognitive process. This offloading deprived metacognitive monitoring of its raw material and weakened the perceived necessity of self-checking, thereby producing a chain from cognitive offloading through reduced metacognitive engagement to metacognitive disengagement. The finding that cognitive offloading only partially mediated the relationship suggests that other mechanisms may also be at work, such as changes in self-efficacy or perceived task responsibility. These possibilities remain open for future investigation. 5 Experiment 3: the causal effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality Experiment 2 provided evidence that cognitive offloading mediates the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. However, because cognitive offloading was measured rather than manipulated, the causal direction remained uncertain. Experiment 3 addressed this limitation by manipulating the degree of cognitive delegation to AI-the core behavioral expression of cognitive offloading in human-AI collaboration-and examining its causal effect on knowledge innovation quality, with metacognitive disengagement as a mediator. Experiment 3 provided causal evidence for the effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement. First, manipulating cognitive offloading produced the expected difference in metacognitive disengagement: participants in the high-delagation condition showed significantly stronger metacognitive disengagement than those in the low-delagation condition. Because cognitive offloading was experimentally manipulated rather than merely measured, these results strengthen the inference that workflow features involving greater delegation to AI lead to stronger metacognitive disengagement. Second, cognitive offloading significantly impaired knowledge innovation quality across all three dimensions. Interestingly, the between-group difference was somewhat smaller for developability than for novelty and usefulness. One interpretation is that AI-generated solutions often appear structurally complete and operationally plausible in the short term, but lack the depth and sustainability that come from genuine iterative reflection. This pattern is consistent with the illusion of competence described by Fan et al. (2025) , in which the fluent output of AI masks underlying deficiencies in quality (Tsakalerou et al., 2026) . Third, metacognitive disengagement partially mediated the effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality. This finding indicates that cognitive offloading damages innovation quality primarily, though not exclusively, by weakening metacognitive planning, monitoring, and reflection. The residual direct effect also suggests that other mechanisms may operate alongside metacognitive disengagement. At the same time, the two workflow conditions inevitably differed in other features such as the detail of AI responses, the amount of independent effort requested, and the allocation of responsibility for core content. The findings should therefore be interpreted as reflecting the combined influence of a high-delegation workflow, within which cognitive offloading is the central feature. Future research could hold these features constant while varying only the degree of cognitive delegation to isolate the unique contribution of cognitive offloading. Consistent with Amabile's (1983) componential theory of creativity, the results imply that when metacognitive skills are no longer exercised in human-AI collaborative tasks, the formal completeness of AI-generated output may conceal a loss of deeper creative quality. Experiment 4 extended the findings of Experiments 1 through 3 by identifying two boundary conditions of the indirect effect from cognitive offloading through metacognitive disengagement to knowledge innovation quality. First, task complexity strengthened the negative indirect effect. Under high task complexity, the indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement was significantly stronger than under low task complexity. This pattern is consistent with the proposition that complex innovation tasks require more extensive metacognitive processing (Campbell, 1988) . When tasks are complex, AI outputs typically serve only as a starting point, and individuals must critically evaluate, integrate, and deeply process AI-generated content. Under such conditions, metacognitive disengagement leads to particularly severe losses in innovation quality. Second, AI literacy buffered the negative indirect effect. Individuals with higher AI literacy maintained relatively higher knowledge innovation quality even under high cognitive offloading, whereas those with lower AI literacy showed stronger negative effects. This finding suggests that the value of AI literacy lies not simply in better technical operation of AI but in the ability to maintain critical distance from AI outputs and to preserve metacognitive vigilance during human-AI collaboration (Long and Magerko, 2020) . Third, the supplementary analyses clarified that neither task complexity nor AI literacy moderated the first-stage path from cognitive offloading to metacognitive disengagement. Instead, both moderators operated at the stage at which metacognitive disengagement translated into innovation quality. This distinction indicates that metacognitive disengagement may arise fairly generally under AI-assisted conditions, but its consequences depend on task characteristics and individual capabilities. For individuals with high AI literacy or for simple tasks, even if metacognitive disengagement occurs, its actual damage to innovation quality is relatively limited; for complex tasks or low-AIliteracy individuals, the same level of metacognitive disengagement leads to more substantial quality loss.
