Of the 981 questionnaires returned, 174 were excluded (30 non-physical-education teachers, 113 with completion times outside the platform limits of 1 to 30 min, and 31 with inconsistent responses) and 807 (82.26%) were valid. The questionnaire was initially sent to teachers at 18 universities in six provinces and municipalities (Sichuan, Guangdong, Chongqing, Beijing, Hainan, and Hunan) and was then circulated through snowball referral. Because the questionnaire was anonymous, respondent-level institutional affiliation was not recorded, and because of problems in the collection and compilation of the gender, age, and teaching-experience data, these variables could not be used. No further sample profile can therefore be reported, and the distribution of participants across universities is unknown; this limits the assessment of representativeness (see Section 5.6). Because all data were collected through self-report at a single time point, the results might be susceptible to common method bias. Harman’s single-factor test was therefore conducted in SPSS 27.0 using an unrotated principal component analysis of all 63 items across the four scales. The first unrotated factor accounted for 19.365% of the total variance, below the 40% threshold. This result alone does not rule out common method variance, because Harman’s test has low sensitivity and does not statistically partial out method effects ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ); common method bias therefore cannot be excluded, and the associations reported below may be inflated or attenuated by shared method variance. More stringent procedures, such as an unmeasured latent method factor analysis or multi-source and multi-wave data, would be needed to examine this issue more rigorously. To examine the structural validity of the four constructs, a four-factor measurement model (perceived AI acceptance, digital well-being, innovative work behavior, and occupational well-being) was tested in AMOS 26.0 using maximum likelihood estimation, with dimension-level mean scores used as observed indicators (item parcels); for occupational well-being, the four indicators were the means of the five items of each of the four JAWS subscales defined by Van Katwyk et al. (2000) , with the two low-pleasure subscales reverse-scored. As shown in Table 2 , the measurement model demonstrated good fit to the data: χ 2 (38) = 43.60, p = 0.246, χ 2 /df = 1.147, GFI = 0.990, AGFI = 0.983, NFI = 0.987, IFI = 0.998, TLI = 0.998, CFI = 0.998, RMSEA = 0.014 (90% CI [0.000, 0.029]), and SRMR = 0.018. All indices met or exceeded recommended thresholds ( χ 2 /df < 3, CFI > 0.95, RMSEA < 0.08, SRMR < 0.08) ( Hu and Bentler, 1999 ). Because parcels can yield more favorable fit than item-level models, these indices should be interpreted with caution (item-level results are reported in Section 4.7). The four indicators of occupational well-being are subscale means of the same instrument, and the subscales could not be distinguished in this sample (Section 4.7), so they reflect one overall construct; their high loadings (0.745–0.817) are therefore expected. analysis.discussion: This study constructed and tested a serial mediation model examining whether perceived AI acceptance is associated with university PE teachers’ occupational well-being through the sequential mediating roles of digital well-being and innovative work behavior. The data were consistent with all four hypotheses, and the pattern of results is compatible with a resource-based interpretation of how favorable technological appraisal may be linked to occupational adaptation in a digitalizing higher-education context. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design, however, the results describe statistical indirect associations and not established psychological mechanisms or temporal processes. This study found that perceived AI acceptance was significantly and positively associated with university PE teachers’ occupational well-being, supporting Hypothesis H1 and aligning with a growing body of evidence documenting positive associations between favorable technology appraisals and occupational adjustment among teachers ( Yi et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ). The association between perceived AI acceptance and occupational well-being was accompanied by indirect associations through both digital well-being and innovative work behavior, which were themselves intercorrelated. From the perspective of Conservation of Resources theory, perceived AI acceptance can be interpreted as a favorable appraisal of a potential job resource, which is consistent with lower anticipated resource loss and with higher levels of resources in digital and behavioral domains ( Hobfoll, 1989 ; Hobfoll et al., 2018 ) (these resource states were not directly measured). Higher levels of such resources are, in turn, associated with more favorable affective experiences of work, consistent with the Job Demands–Resources proposition that job and personal resources are linked to engagement and well-being ( Bakker and Demerouti, 2017 ). Notably, similar to prior chain-mediation research on teacher occupational well-being ( Nong et al., 2022 ), the serial indirect pathway identified in the present study, while statistically reliable, represented a modest proportion of the total effect (11.66%), indicating that the sequence from digital well-being to innovative work behavior accounts for only a modest part of the association between perceived AI acceptance and occupational well-being, and that other factors not measured here are likely to be involved. Given that prosocial and occupational outcomes are typically shaped by numerous factors beyond any single technological appraisal—such as institutional support, professional identity, and workload—the magnitude of the present associations is consistent with the broader literature’s understanding of teacher well-being as a multiply determined outcome, while still carrying meaningful implications for how institutions introduce and scaffold AI tools for PE faculty. This study also found a statistically significant indirect association between perceived AI acceptance and university PE teachers’ occupational well-being through digital well-being, consistent with Hypothesis H2. This result indicates that perceived AI acceptance is not only directly associated with occupational well-being but also shows an indirect association with it through digital well-being (in a statistical sense). One possible interpretation, which these data cannot test directly, is that when AI tools are appraised as useful and easy to operate, teachers may be less likely to experience the technology as an additional demand and may be more likely to adopt selective, adaptive strategies for managing digital information and communication flows ( Gui et al., 2017 ). Consistent with this reasoning, prior organizational research has shown that workplace digitization is associated with reduced digital anxiety, which in turn is linked to enhanced employee well-being ( Han Z. et al., 2025 ). Within a COR framework, a favorable technological appraisal is theoretically linked to a lower anticipated resource cost of digital engagement, which may be related to higher digital well-being as a personal resource that is, in turn, associated with broader occupational well-being ( Hobfoll, 1989 ; Diener et al., 1999 ). Thus, the emotional and cognitive experience of digital demands may be one relevant correlate linking PE teachers’ appraisal of AI and their overall occupational well-being. The results showed that innovative work behavior had a significant indirect association linking perceived AI acceptance and university PE teachers’ occupational well-being, consistent with Hypothesis H3. This finding is compatible with a role for proactive, resource-investing behavior in linking technology appraisal and occupational adaptation, although the cross-sectional data do not establish this role. When PE teachers regard AI tools as beneficial and easy to use, they appear more willing to invest cognitive and behavioral resources in generating, promoting, and realizing novel ideas in their work, consistent with recent evidence that generative AI use is associated with employees’ innovation performance through resource acquisition and integration mechanisms ( Wang et al., 2025 ). Innovative work behavior is, in turn, associated with occupational well-being, plausibly because the successful promotion and realization of novel ideas is linked to experiences of competence, recognition, and positive affect at work ( West and Farr, 1990 ; Janssen, 2000 ). This finding is consistent with prior literature indicating that innovative behavior is associated with individual well-being outcomes ( Amabile, 1988 ), and adds evidence on this association in the domain of AI-related technology appraisal among university PE teachers. Note that innovative work behavior was measured with Janssen’s general scale, which captures idea generation, promotion, and realization in one’s work role; it does not specifically capture teaching or pedagogical innovation. The instructional examples given above are therefore illustrations of how general innovative behavior might appear among PE teachers and not features of what was measured. This study further found a statistically significant serial indirect association through digital well-being and innovative work behavior in sequence, consistent with Hypothesis H4. This pattern is compatible with a cumulative, resource-based sequence: from a favorable technological appraisal, to digital resource sufficiency, to proactive behavioral resource investment, and then to occupational well-being. analysis.methods: The baseline data for Phase 1 were collected from students enrolled at a medical university in China. A total of 1025 medical students (399 male, 626 female) completed the survey, with ages ranging from 16 to 24 years (M = 19.41, SD = 3.207). They were recruited from Sojump, a Chinese online survey platform, for a study titled "A Research of Your Opinions on Smartphone Use." After reading an information sheet describing the study procedures, participants completed the survey in accordance with the provided instructions. All procedures were approved by the Scientific Research Ethics Review Committee of Shanxi Medical University (approval No. 2025038; approval date: January 8, 2025). All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation. For minors (under 18 years), additional written consent was obtained from their legal guardians, along with participant assent directly from the minors themselves. Participants were informed of their right to withdraw at any time without penalty. All data were collected anonymously and stored securely. In Phases 2 and 3, the final longitudinal sample consisted of 668 medical students (61.68% female), with a mean age of 19.64 years (SD = 1.11; range = 17-24). All participants were invited to complete a battery of online self-report measures at two follow-up time points: 4 months (T2) and 8 months (T3) after T1. Of the initial 1025 participants at T1, 668 participants (65%) completed all three waves of data collection and were included in the primary longitudinal analyses. Retention rates were 69% (n = 705) at T2 and 65% (n = 668) at T3. All assessment sessions could be completed from any smartphone with internet access.
analysis.discussion: The present study provides a comprehensive examination of the relationship between CAS and SABA using a multi-method approach that integrates cross-sectional, longitudinal, and machine learning analyses. The results support the proposed metacognitive model of SABA, which was developed by extending and modifying Wells' (2009) S-REF framework of obsessive-compulsive disorders (OCD) to the context of behavioral addictions, demonstrating that CAS is associated with SABA across multiple analytical approaches. A key contribution of this study is the use of RI-CLPM to disentangle between-person stability from within-person fluctuations, revealing that the CAS-SABA relationship operates primarily at the trait level, with worry uniquely emerging as the core domain most consistently associated with both stable comorbidity and dynamic change. This study systematically examined the associations between CAS, including total score and domains, and SABA using a multi-wave longitudinal design with multiple analytical approaches. The findings provide empirical support for the proposed metacognitive model of SABA, demonstrating that CAS total score is primarily associated with SABA at the between-person level, indicating a stable trait-level comorbidity rather than a short-term dynamic process. Among the seven CAS domains, worry uniquely emerged as the most consistent predictor for SABA: it showed the strongest between-person association with SABA and the largest within-person cross-lagged association, with a directional path from worry to SABA. This within-person association remained significant even after controlling for comorbid anxiety and depression, supporting worry as a prospective within-person correlate of SABA. Methodologically, the integration of LCGM, Random Forest, and SHAP analyses provided convergent evidence across person-centered and variable-centered approaches, which extended the RI-CLPM findings by indicating that the relative influence of CAS domains differs across SABA trajectories. Machine learning analyses consistently identified worry as the most influential CAS domain in relation to SABA, ranking first in predicting both high-stable and moderate-decreasing trajectories of SABA, and further suggested a synergistic interaction between worry and substance use, corresponding to a higher likelihood of belonging to the high-stable SABA trajectory. Clinically, the dual-pathway pattern of worry observed in the RI-CLPM suggests worry can serve different functions depending on the target population and time frame. At the trait level, its strong betweenperson association with SABA supports its potential use as a screening marker for identifying high SABA-risk medical students who may benefit from early prevention for SABA. At the state level, its significant withinperson association with SABA suggests that worry fluctuations may serve as a dynamic indicator for monitoring short-term changes in SABA risk. For medical students who have already developed SABA, whether worry represents a candidate target for future intervention research, and whether reducing worry could potentially influence the maintenance of SABA requires confirmation in future experimental studies. Given that the within-person association of worry remained significant after controlling for anxiety and depression, future research could examine whether interventions targeting worry are effective regardless of individuals' current anxiety or depression levels. Future research could employ experimental designs (e.g., randomized controlled trials targeting worry) to further test whether worry prospectively predicts SABA, and whether abbreviated metacognitive therapy is effective in reducing worry and, consequently, alleviating SABA among medical students at both short-term and long-term levels.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the reliance on self-report measures and the specific sample of medical students in China may limit the generalizability of these findings. Future research could replicate these findings using more diverse populations and multimethod assessments (e.g., objective measures such as actual smartphone usage data) to reduce this potential bias. Second, the 35% attrition rate over the three waves needs to be considered when interpreting the findings. Although attrition analyses suggested limited bias (|d| = .168-.196), the reduced sample size may have limited statistical power to detect small effects, particularly at the within-person level. Future research with larger samples and lower attrition rates is needed. Third, although anxiety and depression were controlled as covariates in the RI-CLPM, they were not controlled for in all analyses of this research. Future research could systematically include these covariates across all analytical levels. Fourth, the entropy values for the LCGM (.69-.74) indicated moderate trajectory classification precision, suggesting that the trajectoryspecific results, particularly those involving the low-stable group (n = 84, 12.50%), warrant careful interpretation. Future research with larger samples and more waves of data is needed to replicate and refine these trajectory classifications. Fifth, the SABAS uses a single item per addiction criterion, which may limit measurement precision. The use of a 6-point Likert format for both the SABAS and MCASS, while intended to reduce neutral midpoint bias, may have influenced response distributions and warrant consideration when interpreting the findings. Although the SABAS has been validated as a brief screening tool, future research could employ multiitem measures for greater reliability. Sixth, the two-step factor-score sensitivity analysis partially accounted for measurement error in CAS. However, the CAS latent measurement model showed relatively poor fit, and the factor loadings for substance use (λ = .29-.33) and worry (λ = .46-.50) were relatively low, suggesting these domains were less well represented by the latent factor. Furthermore, the strict one-step latent RI-CLPM did not converge, and SABA remained a unidimensional construct represented by an observed total score. Estimating a fully latent RI-CLPM with seven indicators across three waves involves a large number of parameters, which may have contributed to the estimation difficulty. Therefore, measurement error was not fully addressed, and the factor-score analyses represent limited, exploratory sensitivity checks. Future research with larger samples and more stable measurement models may be needed to estimate fully latent RI-CLPMs that better account for measurement error in CAS. Seventh, the measurement invariance results warrant consideration, as the configural models for SABAS and MCASS showed relatively weak fit, and SABAS achieved partial rather than full scalar invariance. Therefore, these results provide qualified, rather than definitive, evidence of measurement equivalence across time. Eighth, the three-wave longitudinal design constrained the precision of growth trajectory estimation. Future research with more frequent assessments (e.g., ecological momentary assessment) could further clarify the short-term dynamic relationship between worry and SABA. Ninth, although RI-CLPM provides a more stringent test of temporal precedence than traditional CLPM, it does not establish causation. Future research could employ experimental designs, such as randomized controlled trials targeting worry, to further test whether worry prospectively predicts SABA, and whether abbreviated metacognitive therapy is effective.

reading.interpretation: We first introduce a dataset of human answers in 6 common language (Fig. 1 ) and vision (Fig. 3 ) tasks to evaluate the ability of algorithms to imitate humans. The dataset also includes answers from state-of-the-art AI algorithms (Table S1 ). Using the human and machine answers, we conducted Turing-like tests, showing that current algorithms are not far from being able to imitate humans in these tasks (Fig. 4A-C , G-I , Fig. S5A , C , E , Fig. S15A , C , E ). In contrast to human judges, even simple machine judges can distinguish human from machine answers (Fig. 4D-F , J-L , Fig. S5B , D , F Fig. S15B , D , F ). The Turing test has been extensively discussed, and contested, as a means to assess general intelligence. Our work is not intended as an evaluation of intelligence or to contribute to the discussion of Turing tests to quantify intelligence. Imitating humans can benefit humanity in many situations where we want to align machine and human outputs, such as in emulating expert decisions. However, imitating humans can also be used for evil, as in the dissemination of fake information, phishing attempts, or other scams. Regardless of whether Turing tests are good or bad metrics of intelligence, it is of high practical importance to assess whether algorithms can imitate humans or not. In some cases, we summarized results using the overall imitation detectability metric. It is important to emphasize that this summary metric does not differentiate between the two types of classification errors: (1) False Negatives -A human response misclassified as machine-generated. (2) False Positives -A machine response misclassified as human-generated. analysis.discussion: We first introduce a dataset of human answers in 6 common language (Fig. 1 ) and vision (Fig. 3 ) tasks to evaluate the ability of algorithms to imitate humans. The dataset also includes answers from state-of-the-art AI algorithms (Table S1 ). Using the human and machine answers, we conducted Turing-like tests, showing that current algorithms are not far from being able to imitate humans in these tasks (Fig. 4A-C , G-I , Fig. S5A , C , E , Fig. S15A , C , E ). In contrast to human judges, even simple machine judges can distinguish human from machine answers (Fig. 4D-F , J-L , Fig. S5B , D , F Fig. S15B , D , F ). The Turing test has been extensively discussed, and contested, as a means to assess general intelligence. Our work is not intended as an evaluation of intelligence or to contribute to the discussion of Turing tests to quantify intelligence. Imitating humans can benefit humanity in many situations where we want to align machine and human outputs, such as in emulating expert decisions. However, imitating humans can also be used for evil, as in the dissemination of fake information, phishing attempts, or other scams. Regardless of whether Turing tests are good or bad metrics of intelligence, it is of high practical importance to assess whether algorithms can imitate humans or not. In some cases, we summarized results using the overall imitation detectability metric. It is important to emphasize that this summary metric does not differentiate between the two types of classification errors: (1) False Negatives -A human response misclassified as machine-generated. (2) False Positives -A machine response misclassified as human-generated. Understanding the distinction between these two error types is important for interpreting decision-making by human and machine judges. Moreover, in real-world applications, these errors may have different consequences. For example, misclassifying a machine as a human might be more problematic than misclassifying a human as a machine if the goal is to reliably detect AI-generated content. We present confusion matrices throughout to complement the imitation detectability scores and quantify the two types of errors. One approach towards mitigating the risks from evil human imitators is to build AI judges that can distinguish true human answers. The results presented here show that even simple AI judges like the ones introduced here can generally do a better job than human judges in detecting machine answers for the current tasks. There will likely continue to be an arms race between the development of better imitators and better detectors. In most of the Turing-like tests presented here, AI judges were explicitly trained to classify responses from humans versus AIs, while human judges received no explicit training. However, we also presented results using ChatGPT-4o, a state-of-the-art, off-the-shelf, multimodal model. We evaluated ChatGPT-4o in zero-shot Turing-like tests across all six tasks. This unified, multi-modal model can distinguish between human and machine-generated responses with above-chance accuracy, even without any explicit training. These observations also raise the possibility that humans may be trained to better recognize machine answers. In support of this hypothesis, when human judges received training in the form of trial-by-trial feedback, they showed improved accuracy in identifying human-generated responses. By and large, humans have lived in a world without good human imitators and did not have to worry too much about the possibility of machines emulating humans, other than in famous works of fiction. This situation is changing rapidly and may lead to the need to educate human judges. An algorithm's ability to imitate humans does not necessarily correlate with traditional performance metrics like accuracy. Consider a simple scenario of an image with a highly occluded dog that is hard to see, and both machines and humans interpret the object to be a wolf. Both would be wrong, but the machine would be adequately imitating humans. Conversely, the example in Fig. S14C for the Image captioning task. This example shows that both machines and humans can provide correct answers, but the algorithm does not fully imitate how humans interpret the image. Thus, M and H can be wrong, and M can adequately imitate H; M and H can also both be right and M fail to adequately imitate H. Being right or wrong is not the same as imitation. Turing-like tests provide a complementary assessment to existing benchmarking frameworks for AI algorithms. Comparisons between models in Turing-like tests also provide insights helpful for developing future AI models that can better align with humans. We refer to the evaluations in our study as "Turing-like" to emphasize that they are not identical to Turing's original description [44] . Turing did not spell out the implementation details of his tests, perhaps because he did not imagine at the time that these tests could be truly implemented, barely a few decades later. The datasets and evaluations introduced here are extensive (72, 191 Turing-like test trials, 636 humans contributing to the dataset, and 1,916 human judges). Yet, these evaluations barely scratch the surface of what needs to be evaluated. There are essentially infinite possible Turing-like tests. Each algorithm and each task can be evaluated in terms of imitation capabilities. Even within a particular task, there are multiple ways of instantiating a Turing-like test. The results of a Turing-like test depend on the task, the algorithm, how the question is formulated, the demographics of the human agent, the characteristics of the human judge, and many other variables. Such variations are particularly evident in the context of conversation tasks where the topic, medium, length, format, instructions, agent and judge expertise, and agent and judge demographics, can lead to different results [32] , [34] , [37] , [38] , [39] , [40] . For example, the conversation topic and participant expertise can be critical: one could conduct the conversation focusing exclusively on medieval history, string theory, or basketball games as conversation topics and agents/judges with or without domain-specific knowledge may perform differently. However, the topic-agnostic formulation is relevant to many (but certainly not all) real-world scenarios. The results presented here further emphasize the importance of integrative benchmarks. The current work is not intended as an exhaustive assessment of every conceivable task. We do not believe such a complete characterization is even feasible in practice. Instead, we focus on a subset of task formulations that arise naturally in everyday contexts. For instance, in conversational tasks, one might imagine an exchange between two agents on a social media platform, with an observer attempting to determine whether both, one, or neither of the participants is human. We also implemented and evaluated an online version of the conversation task that is closer to the original formulation of the Turing task. The results from the online test with adversarial prompting differ from those of the offline, non-adversarial formulation. These are distinct experiments based on contrasting formats and underlying assumptions, which naturally lead to different outcomes, further emphasizing that the details of how the Turing tests are defined matter. The findings underscore that Turing-like test results can vary widely

title: Intention Tracking [iOS] — one sec
evidence: Product documentation; no independent effectiveness assessment
preview: The one sec app can prompt people to state why they are opening a distracting app. This introduces a moment of reflection at the point of a potentially automatic habit.

editorial_notes.argument: Product documentation describes an intention picker before access to an app. The tool asks people to clarify their reason for opening it.
editorial_notes.design_relevance: Compare deliberate friction against hard blocking and passive tracking. Measure subsequent app-opening decisions, sense of autonomy, and irritation from extra prompts.
editorial_notes.caveat: Product documentation is a description of features, not independently established evidence of effectiveness.

longform.thesis: Product documentation describes an intention picker before access to an app. The tool asks people to clarify their reason for opening it.
longform.reasoning: The product introduces a small decision point before an app opens. Its mechanism is deliberate friction and self-reflection, rather than continuous measurement of attention.
longform.examples: The described intention picker asks what a person wants to do before entering a distracting app. A design comparison would need to distinguish noticing an intention from actually changing subsequent behavior.
longform.tension: Additional friction may discourage automatic use, but can also become irritating or easy to ignore. The product description does not establish which outcome dominates.
longform.implications: Compare deliberate friction against hard blocking and passive tracking. Measure subsequent app-opening decisions, sense of autonomy, and irritation from extra prompts.
longform.open_question: Does an intention prompt change what people do next, or merely add an extra tap?
longform.qualification: Product documentation is a description of features, not independently established evidence of effectiveness.
